papers.title: Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package: A Stable Machine-Readable Contract for Alignment Research and System Design
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Representation alignment research now spans multimodal, cross-lingual, cross-domain, multi-view, and model-to-model systems, with a rapidly expanding range of models, losses, matching procedures, and training strategies. However, the design decisions that determine whether an alignment strategy is appropriate for a particular problem are often implicit in technical choices or scattered across papers, code, experiments, and local discussion. A method name and its reported performance may show what was used and how it performed without making clear what compatibility was intended, what correspondence was assumed, what information should remain distinct, or why those choices fit the problem. This makes it harder to design systems around the requirements of the problem, compare methods at a common design level, and carry design intent reliably into implementation. Existing resources support important parts of this work. Surveys and taxonomies help researchers understand which alignment methods and research families have been developed. Experiment platforms record what was run and how it performed, while provenance and documentation standards capture where artifacts came from, how they were produced, and how they are intended to be used. These resources make methods, experiments, and artifacts easier to find, reproduce, and inspect. The design rationale connecting a particular problem to a particular form of alignment, however, can remain embedded in local terminology, technical choices, and project-specific documentation. As a result, knowledge generated through earlier design work can remain difficult to compare across projects, transfer between teams, or accumulate into a reusable body of knowledge. The Representation Alignment Compass (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22096467) provides a compact and relatively stable design-level reference for the high-leverage commitments that determine what form of alignment a problem requires. The Representation Alignment Compass Core Semantic Package (RAC-CORE) makes this reference machine-readable and persistent, allowing alignment commitments, context, evidence, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation artifacts to remain connected through a shared semantic structure as methods and implementations evolve. This provides a common basis for explicit design, coherent interpretation of a changing field, cumulative evidence across projects, and shared reasoning across researchers, teams, tools, and computational agents. Theoretical Framework, Core Package, and Practical Companion RAC-CORE is the machine-readable component of a broader three-resource Representation Alignment architecture. This Zenodo record contains RAC-CORE only; the Theoretical Framework and Practical Companion are separate resources. The framework defines the conceptual design semantics, RAC-CORE preserves those semantics in machine-readable records, and the Practical Companion supports their practical application. Theoretical Framework. Use the published Representation Alignment Compass when the primary need is to understand representation alignment, compare design alternatives, or reason about the high-leverage commitments that should shape a research or system-design problem. It remains authoritative for the conceptual architecture, category meanings, and design logic. Core Semantic Package. Use RAC-CORE when those commitments need to become persistent machine-readable records that can be reviewed, exchanged, versioned, linked to evidence or execution, or reused across projects and computational workflows. RAC-CORE is authoritative for machine-readable semantics and conformance. Practical Companion. The Practical Companion, when released separately on GitHub, will provide richer worked examples, guided authoring, templates, workbenches, integration utilities, and other practice-facing support. It will remain pinned to an exact RAC-CORE release while leaving the conceptual framework and Core semantics unchanged. Core Values 1. Making Alignment Designs Explicit and Reviewable RAC-CORE turns the high-leverage commitments identified through the theoretical framework into an explicit, context-scoped design record. Problem conditions, selected configurations, unresolved choices, rationale, and proposed technical realizations can be examined together rather than reconstructed from separate artifacts. Researchers and system designers can use this record to evaluate whether a design is coherent with its intended purpose and constraints, compare candidate configurations, revise specific commitments, and carry the design reliably into implementation or handoff. The theoretical framework supports the reasoning; RAC-CORE preserves the resulting design state in a form that can be reviewed, versioned, and continued. 2. Maintaining a Coherent and Evolvable Alignment Knowledge Structure Alignment methods, models, losses, and implementations can change rapidly while the higher-level design commitments they realize remain comparatively stable. RAC-CORE allows these technical objects to remain externally versioned while linking them to a persistent alignment architecture. New work can therefore be incorporated into an existing body of knowledge rather than creating another isolated technical category, and users can compare contributions at the level of alignment design rather than method name alone. The structure remains stable where its design distinctions continue to hold, while recurring evidence of genuinely new alignment logic can motivate a governed Core revision. This provides a stable basis for building a coherent and evolvable knowledge structure across alignment work. 3. Building an Evidence Base for Cumulative Learning and Long-Horizon Planning Learning across projects requires more than preserving individual results; experiences must be expressed in a form that allows them to be related across changing methods and contexts. RAC-CORE keeps literature interpretations, intended designs, executed configurations, and evaluation evidence distinguishable but linkable under a stable semantic reference. As reviewed and traceable records accumulate, heterogeneous projects can be represented as structured evidence that can later be assessed for comparability, synthesis, and recurring design patterns under separately governed analysis. This evidence can support later synthesis, diagnosis, meta-level learning, and long-horizon planning under separately governed analytical processes. RAC-CORE does not supply the learned conclusions itself; it provides the common reference structure through which past experience can become usable evidence for future reasoning. 4. Preserving Shared Alignment Semantics Across Projects, Teams, and Agents RAC-CORE provides a common semantic contract for alignment work that moves across projects, researchers, teams, software tools, and computational agents. Canonical identities remain tied to their context, scope, evidence, provenance, uncertainty, and governing release, so records can be exchanged without relying on local terminology or undocumented assumptions to recover their meaning. This supports reliable handoff, cross-project synthesis, accountable revision, machine-assisted review, and long-horizon human–agent collaboration while allowing participants to retain their own methods, datasets, and implementation environments. Supported Tasks RAC-CORE supports two peer machine tasks built on the same theoretical coordinates but representing different epistemic objects. RAC-MAP — Represent an Existing Alignment Design from Evidence Use RAC-MAP when an alignment design already exists and must be interpreted from evidence. The evidence may come from a publication or from direct observation of an executed system, according to the channels defined by the released contract. A RAC-MAP record captures the bounded source being interpreted, the relevant context, the alignment commitments and configurations supported by the evidence, provenance, and the limits of permissible inference. It is designed to preserve partial knowledge without forcing unsupported completion. Publication-derived interpretation and execution-grounded observation remain distinguishable, so what a paper claims and what a system actually executes can be recorded separately. Typical uses include literature and method mapping, system inspection, systematic review, evidence-synthesis datasets, design-history reconstruction, and the construction of reusable alignment-design corpora. RAC-DESIGN — Represent an Intended Alignment Design Use RAC-DESIGN when an alignment strategy is being formulated, reviewed, handed off, or revised. A RAC-DESIGN record captures the problem context, intended alignment commitments, candidate configurations, rationale, unresolved choices, and proposed technical realizations. Concrete methods and implementations remain external objects, allowing technical alternatives to change without redefining the Compass. After implementation, the intended design can be linked to an execution-grounded RAC-MAP and to the associated implementation and evaluation evidence. Typical uses include research planning, system-design specification, design review, team or agent handoff, versioned revision, and traceability from an intended alignment route to its realized form. Downstream Comparison and Learning Conformant RAC records provide a common basis for later comparison, aggregation, visualization, and learning. Shared semantic coordinates make it possible to examine recurring commitments and differences across records, while preserved context and epistemic status help determine whether those records are meaningfully comparable. Any ranking, recommendation, learned tendency, or design-selection procedure remains a downstream analytical responsibility with its own evidence, assumptions, and governance. How to Use RAC-CORE RAC-CORE is used in two primary ways: to represent an existing alignment design

papers.title: AI‐Driven Rational Design of Nanotherapeutics for Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
papers.venue: Medicinal Research Reviews
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a formidable malignancy characterized by late diagnosis, high recurrence rates, and pronounced chemoresistance. While nanoparticle-based drug delivery systems (NDDS) offer theoretical advantages over conventional therapies, their clinical translation in PDAC has been severely limited. The dense desmoplastic stroma, elevated interstitial fluid pressure, and hypovascularity effectively neutralize the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect, restricting passive nanoparticle penetration. Consequently, the therapeutic paradigm is shifting from indiscriminate stromal depletion-which paradoxically accelerates metastasis-to stromal normalization and immune microenvironment reprogramming. This review comprehensively evaluates advanced NDDS platforms, highlighting transcytosis-triggering active targeting, stimuli-responsive carriers, and multimodal theranostic systems designed to bypass physical barriers and convert immunologically "cold" tumors to "hot." Furthermore, we analyze the expanding role of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in predicting synergistic drug combinations and optimizing nanoparticle physicochemical properties. Crucially, we critique current epistemic limitations in AI-driven nanomedicine, particularly data sparsity and the reliance on 2D preclinical models, emphasizing the necessity of 3D patient-derived organoid validation. By integrating rational NDDS design with AI and biomarker-driven strategies, this review maps the essential pathways toward personalized nanotherapeutics for PDAC.

papers.title: Multimodal machine learning-supported comprehensive evaluation of tourism experience
papers.venue: Discover Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: Tourism experiences are multidimensional as they are influenced by the environmental, cultural and emotional factors. The current tourism analytics methods are based on unimodal data sources (surveys or textual reviews), which creates unimodal bias, cross-modal interaction, and limits the interpretability of the patterns of tourist satisfaction. To overcome these shortcomings, this study suggests a multi-modal machine learning (ML)-based model to evaluate tourism satisfaction comprehensively. It uses Multimodal Tourism Experience Dataset, which consists of 18,300 instances and were gathered on Kaggle; each sample consists of a tourist image, a user-generated review, and a five-point satisfaction rating. The image processing includes Gaussian filters and normalization, and numerical ratings are normalized by the MinMax normalization to guarantee consistency. Sentiment features of texts are obtained by means of Bidirectional Encoder Representations of Transformers (BERT) model, aesthetic and environmental representations are obtained by means of images with the help of a pretrained ResNet model. The extracted modality-specific features are integrated through an early feature-level fusion strategy to construct unified multimodal representation. The proposed Dynamic Differential Annealed Optimized Efficient Categorical Boosting (DDA-ECatBoost) model employs differential annealing to achieve stable convergence, robust hyperparameter tuning, and enhanced predictive capability. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance, achieving an accuracy of 0.9768, precision of 0.9647, recall of 0.9555, and an F1-score of 0.9651. Feature importance analysis reveals that comfort and visual appeal are key determinants of tourist satisfaction. Research demonstrates the effectiveness of multimodal data fusion combined with interpretable ML in enhancing tourism satisfaction analysis. It provides valuable insights for destination planners, cultural heritage managers, and tourism marketers aiming to improve visitor satisfaction.

papers.title: Multimodal Data Implicit Semantic Association Mining
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the extraction of implicit semantic associations from multimodal data. The core claim is that humans inherently connect concepts across different modalities (e.g., images, text, audio) in subtle ways. We propose a novel framework leveraging deep learning to learn modality-specific representations and graph neural networks (GNNs) to uncover hidden relationships between these representations. The system aims to move beyond superficial correlations to identify deeper semantic connections, ultimately contributing to a better understanding of human cognition and enhancing information retrieval systems. The key mechanism involves mapping different modalities into a shared embedding space and then utilizing GNNs to propagate information and identify associated nodes. Our approach differs significantly from existing methods that primarily focus on feature-level correlations, offering a more nuanced perspective on multimodal data analysis. We present a methodology for automatically discovering these latent relationships, providing a foundation for applications such as personalized recommendation systems, enhanced search engines, and cognitive modeling. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in identifying complex semantic associations that are not readily apparent through traditional analysis techniques.

papers.title: Development of a Deep Learning Model for Audio Question Answering (AQA)
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents a high-efficiency multimodal framework designed for Audio Question Answering (AQA). To overcome standard CPU and disk I/O bottlenecks, the architecture implements a zero-I/O data pipeline that pre-processes and caches 10,686 samples directly into the 48 GB VRAM of an NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPU during initialization. The model combines a 2D Residual Network (ResNet) audio encoder with an unfrozen 6-layer BERT-base text encoder using a Bilinear Gated Fusion mechanism. Trained across 15 epochs with EMA weight stabilization, the system achieves an extraction throughput of 128-131 files per second and epoch durations of 30-40 seconds, establishing a robust baseline for multimodal acoustic reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Developing Children’s Curiosity-Driven Learning in Early Childhood Education and Care: A Process-Oriented Scaffolding Framework
papers.venue: OpenAlex
papers.abstract: Curiosity-driven learning is widely valued in Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC), yet systematic accounts of how educators can support both learning through curiosity and children’s propensity for curiosity, here collectively referred to as the development of curiosity-driven learning, remain limited. To address this gap, this article proposes the Scaffolding of Curiosity-Driven Learning (SCDL) framework, which integrates curiosity research with scaffolding theory to provide a process-oriented account of how different forms of scaffolding may support children across phases of curiosity-driven learning. Building on this account, the framework articulates a theory of change whereby scaffolding calibrated to the child’s current phase, informational needs, knowledge, and competence may facilitate learning through curiosity and, over time, strengthen children’s propensity for curiosity. For the latter, the framework hypothesizes two pathways through which ECEC contexts may contribute to such development: repeated scaffolded curiosity-driven learning and scaffolding information-gap recognition. This article also presents a multimodal analysis of a naturally occurring teacher–child interaction to demonstrate the SCDL framework’s analytical application and its potential for examining how curiosity-driven learning may be scaffolded in ECEC practice. In sum, the SCDL framework provides an initial theoretically grounded basis for conceptualizing and systematically examining curiosity-driven learning in ECEC, including the formulation and testing of hypothesized mechanisms and pathways through which its development may be supported. If empirically supported, the framework may also help inform pedagogical interventions, professional development, and measures of curiosity-supportive process quality.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Based Framework for Student Engagement Assessment in Classroom Environments
papers.venue: Cognitive Computation
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
papers.abstract: Student distraction remains a critical barrier to effective learning in classroom environments, yet existing detection methods relying on manual observation or post-session feedback are inherently subjective, time-intensive, and ill-suited for real-time adaptive teaching. This study presents the Artificially Intelligent Technology for Student Engagement Assessment in Classroom Environments (AI-TEACH), a novel co-teacher paradigm that automatically identifies and quantifies student distraction through multimodal fusion of asynchronized audio and video streams captured via classroom surveillance cameras. AI-TEACH integrates YOLO-NAS and ByteTrack for real-time student detection and tracking, MediaPipe for behavioral cue extraction, and Silero-VAD with Wav2Vec2-SVM for audio-based emotional distraction classification; a BiLSTM network fuses these multimodal features to generate per-incident severity scores, and a session-wide engagement report accessible through an interactive instructor dashboard. The framework was validated on a curated dataset of classroom recordings and further evaluated through a controlled experiment involving 200 students divided into experimental and control groups, achieving 90% accuracy and 92% recall in distraction detection. Compared with existing unimodal and non-real-time approaches, AI-TEACH offers a more accurate, scalable, and immediately actionable solution for objective student engagement monitoring in modern classroom practice, with direct implications for data-informed pedagogy and inclusive education.

papers.title: Learning as Graph Traversal
papers.venue: OpenAlex
papers.abstract: Large text corpora rarely arrive with the structure a reader needs to navigate them. We present an end-to-end system that induces navigable trails through a flat collection of 323,552 quizbowl questions — short academic quiz texts, each with a canonical answer but no authored links — and serves them to learners through a deployed, multimodal study platform. An offline pipeline segments each question into sentences, embeds them with an instruction-tuned encoder, and clusters each answer’s sentences into concept nodes. Rather than linking concepts by co-occurrence, we order them with optimal leaf ordering (OLO) over their embedding hierarchy, producing, for each subject and difficulty level, a single guided tour that minimizes the total dissimilarity between consecutive concepts. Each tour is at once the navigable structure and the first-exposure sequence; an FSRS-7 spaced-repetition scheduler then governs revisitation at concept granularity. The platform scaffolds each encounter along a five-level ladder of fading support, from highlighted reading with synchronized audio to audio-only recall. The pipeline and platform are the artifacts. A sampled transition audit finds 96% of trail steps land on a related concept; a formative usage observation shows recall accuracy rising with repeated spaced encounters. Establishing pedagogical efficacy remains future work.

papers.title: Diagnosing Administrative Burden in Rural Population-Administration and Civil-Registration Services: A Theory to Practice Conceptual Review for Multimodal Territories
papers.venue: Green Social International Journal of Law and Civil Affairs
papers.abstract: Rural population-administration and civil-registration services in multimodal territories present a public administration problem because documentary requirements, service locations, channel arrangements, and correction pathways may distribute procedural work unevenly between government and citizens. This article develops a source-traceable translation of Administrative Burden Theory for that problem. A theory-focused narrative literature review used six documented Scopus search runs conducted on 16 August 2026. From 10,273 raw records, deduplication and screening produced 45 full-text candidates; 21 eligible peer-reviewed journal articles were retrieved, verified in full text, and included. Qualitative-interpretive synthesis reconstructed the theory’s learning, compliance, and psychological costs, compared applications and criticisms, and traced every proposed practice domain from theory through evidence, interpretation, and boundary conditions. The review yields five domains: navigable information and procedural clarity; consolidated mobility and transaction access; documentary continuity and corrective pathways; choice-preserving hybrid channels and governed assistance; and dignified, differentiated administrative encounters. Together they form a theory-to-practice translation framework that treats territorial conditions as administratively consequential only when service design converts them into required search, travel, waiting, coordination, correction, or psychological costs. The contribution is conceptual and translational rather than theoretical. The framework guides diagnosis and option selection but does not establish current burden prevalence or intervention effectiveness in Sembakung Atulai or other rural jurisdictions.

papers.title: ##基于多模态隐式语义关联的知识图谱生成
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to knowledge graph generation leveraging the inherent semantic relationships within multimodal data. The core idea is to automatically construct richer and more accurate knowledge graphs by analyzing implicit semantic associations across diverse data modalities such as text, images, and audio. We employ a deep learning-based cross-modal representation learning framework to extract latent semantic information from each modality and then utilize association rule mining algorithms to uncover hidden relationships. This method significantly reduces the reliance on manual annotation, offering a scalable and automated solution for knowledge graph construction. We present a detailed explanation of the methodology, highlighting the key components and their interactions. The proposed approach demonstrates potential for generating more comprehensive and reliable knowledge graphs compared to traditional methods.

papers.title: LINGUISTIC SCAFFOLDING IN CLIL MATHEMATICS: A THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK FOR INSTRUCTIONAL DESIGN
papers.venue: OpenAlex
papers.abstract: This paper examines cognitive demands in Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) mathematics, where students process mathematical logic and academic English. A key challenge involves distinguishing conceptual misunderstanding from linguistic barriers. Drawing upon Cognitive Load Theory, the research analyzes secondary education instructional materials. The study suggests a three-step linguistic scaffolding model: vocabulary priming, syntactic simplification, and multimodal representation. This framework aims to help manage cognitive load, potentially supporting bilingual mathematics acquisition.

papers.title: Ethical Asymmetry in Human-Robot Interaction – An Empirical Test of Sparrow’s Hypothesis
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Human-Robot Interaction
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Psychology of Moral and Emotional Judgment
papers.abstract: The ethics of human-robot interaction (HRI) have been discussed extensively based on three traditional frameworks: deontology, consequentialism, and virtue ethics. We conducted a mixed within/between experiment to investigate Sparrow's proposed ethical asymmetry hypothesis in human treatment of robots. The moral permissibility of action (MPA) was manipulated as a subject grouping variable, and virtue type (prudence, justice, courage, and temperance) was controlled as a within-subjects factor. We tested moral stimuli using an online questionnaire with Perceived Moral Permissibility of Action (PMPA) and Perceived Virtue Scores (PVS) as response measures. The PVS measure was based on an adaptation of the established Questionnaire on Cardinal Virtues (QCV), while the PMPA was based on Malle et al. [43] work. We found that the MPA significantly influenced the PMPA and perceived virtue scores. The best-fitting model to describe the relationship between PMPA and PVS was cubic, which is symmetrical in nature. Our study did not confirm Sparrow's asymmetry hypothesis. The adaptation of the QCV is expected to have utility for future studies, pending additional psychometric property assessments.

papers.title: Resilient localization for mobile robots using multi-sensor fusion and a hybrid learning-filtering framework
papers.venue: Scientific Reports
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate and resilient localization is important for autonomous mobile robots in the real world along with diverse environments. Single-sensor approaches are vulnerable to noise and failures and unreliability for diverse environments. In this study, a novel technique is presented with a comprehensive multi-sensor fusion framework using a filter technique and machine learning to enhance localization accuracy and resilience. Different sensors are fused with different characteristics, so the system can execute in different environments, such as daytime, nighttime, indoor, and outdoor, using LiDAR, visual cameras, GPS, UWB, and IMU sensors. In this study, three strategies are used: (i) a baseline standard Extended Kalman Filter (EKF); (ii) a novel dual-stage iterative EKF that refines LiDAR-Inertial Odometry (LIO) and Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) separately; and (iii) a hybrid learning and filtering technique, where Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is used for predicting robot velocities/positions, while EKF is employed for integrating the predicted result. Significant improvements were demonstrated through experimental validation on a simulated robot in ROS-Gazebo. The value of the localization error of the standard EKF was 0.226 m (Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)). The RMSE of post-EKF in dual-stage EKF are better than standard EKF with a value of 0.014 m. The hybrid LSTM-EKF model achieved an RMSE of 0.197 m during failures compared to 0.144 m during smooth operation. This framework offers a scalable solution for reliable autonomous navigation by greatly improving localization accuracy and resilience against sensor failure and degradation.

papers.title: Execution Governance 4.0: From Authorization-Bound Execution to Governed Effect Fabrics
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Execution Governance 4.0 (EG4) extends Execution Governance from authorization-bound execution at an individual effect boundary to the preservation of current, non-expanding, revocable, and independently verifiable authority across a distributed Governed Effect Fabric. EG4 addresses a structural problem in increasingly autonomous and distributed systems: local authentication, authorization, policy compliance, valid credentials, or individually permitted actions do not necessarily establish that the final consequential effect still possesses a coherent and current authority path after authority has been delegated, translated, cached, re-expressed, revoked, or carried across agents, protocols, organizations, versions, services, and physical control points. EG4 does not replace the Six Conditions or the EG3 authorization-bound commitment invariant, and it introduces no seventh live normative condition. Instead, it composes over EG3 with a fabric-level engineering predicate, Fabric Integrity, comprising six properties: Current Authority Path Semantic Non-Expansion Revocation Closure Runtime Continuity Commit-Surface Completeness Witnessed Closure Four primary governance objects structure the architecture: the Governance Contract, Authority Graph, Runtime Witness, and Commit Evidence Package (CEP). Together, they provide a profile-defined way to preserve authority semantics and currentness across heterogeneous execution boundaries while making stale authority, semantic expansion, unresolved conflict, material runtime drift, or unmediated commit paths detectable and capable of failing closed or triggering re-authorization. The central architectural proposition is: “Authority must survive translation without expansion.” EG4 is deliberately broader than AI. The governed object is the consequential external effect, not a model, prompt, reasoning trace, or software agent as such. The architecture is therefore applicable to autonomous workflows, AI agents, programmable finance, software-controlled infrastructure, robotics, IoT, industrial control, and other cyber-physical systems in which distributed capabilities can create real-world consequences. Version 0.3.8 is an evidence-synchronized, prior-art-hardened research-architecture release. It preserves the EG4 architecture semantics established in the earlier v0.3.6 series while incorporating a stronger cumulative evidence programme. The bounded EG4 common core carrying Semantic Non-Expansion, Revocation and live-current-state obligations was externally reproduced on three tester-controlled heterogeneous edge platforms: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (ARM64, Ubuntu 24.04 / ROS 2 Jazzy), Orange Pi 5B (ARM64, Ubuntu 22.04 / ROS 2 Humble), and Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W (32-bit ARMv7, Raspbian Bookworm constrained profile). Across the common tested core, the evidence sets produced materially identical normalized outcomes, including Gate3B TLC PASS (195 generated states, 66 distinct states, depth 8), six intended guard-ablation counterexamples, 37/37 reference-evaluator tests, 32/32 falsification vectors, Gate4A 15/15, and Gate4C 16/16 with dynamic revocation blocked as expected. The release also incorporates ERP-1D v0.1.2, in which one eligible Gate4C release was carried through an authenticated ESP32-S3 enforcement endpoint to a board-local RGB-LED physical effect. All 10 pre-registered HIL vectors passed and the endpoint actuation counter advanced exactly once. The nominal eligible vector produced one visually observed effect, while authority failure, dynamic revocation, exact-effect mutation, independent safety veto, HMAC tamper, replay, expiry, wrong-session, and wrong-target vectors produced no additional actuation. EG4 also provides a machine-readable research seam comprising a candidate EG4-Core v0.1 semantic kernel, Minimal Digital Fabric Profile v0.1, profile-bounded JSON Schemas, a bounded executable counterexample model, an author-controlled reference implementation, conformance tests, an OpenAPI surface, and a version-pinned research endpoint. The prior-art boundary is intentionally conservative. EG4 does not claim invention of authentication, delegation, authorization evidence, authority provenance graphs, governance contracts, complete mediation, least privilege, revocation, semantic interoperability, cryptographic receipts, runtime authorization, or conformance testing in isolation. Related standards and research—including MCP, A2A, WIMSE, OAuth Rich Authorization Requests, Transaction Tokens, SCITT, Microsoft Agent Hooks, Execution-Time Authorization, Proof of Execution, LATTICE, AID-Guard, Quipu and related work—are treated as substrates, adjacent architectures, or prior-art pressure rather than as endorsements of EG. The strongest defensible EG4 claim is therefore not that every component mechanism is new. It is the effect-fabric composition of current rooted authority, semantic non-expansion, descendant revocation closure, runtime continuity, declared commit-surface mediation, exact-effect commitment, and independently checkable closure across heterogeneous consequential action chains. Evidence and maturity boundary: EG4 v0.3.8 is a publication-ready independent research and pre-standardization architecture. The reported results are bounded research evidence. They do not constitute full formal verification of EG4, an independent reimplementation from specification, universal interoperability proof, open-world commit-surface completeness, accredited laboratory validation, functional-safety certification, production assurance, legal authorization, compliance determination, or institutional endorsement.

papers.title: SynTactiq Tactile Contact Dataset — Free Sample (200K synthetic contacts, v0.2.0)
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Synthetic tactile contact dataset generated with physics-based simulation (MuJoCo) for robot slip detection, grasp stability and sim-to-real transfer research. This free sample guarantees 200,000+ contact samples across 608 simulated runs spanning 13 object materials × 5 contact scenarios (press, slide, stick-slip, roll, twist). Each contact row stores normal force, two tangential force components, friction coefficients and contact position, exported in a documented HDF5 schema with per-run provenance, checksums and a JSON manifest. Slip labels are derivable from the Coulomb friction-cone criterion (|Ft| ≥ μ·Fn), matching the label convention of real Meta DIGIT benchmarks. Use cases: pre-training tactile models before touching hardware, sim-to-real domain-gap studies, dataset curation research. Live mirrors: Hugging Face and Kaggle. Commercial license (up to 1M contacts): jacopo.sardella@gmail.com

papers.title: International Automation Rent and Destination Equalisation Accord: A Treaty Working Draft with an Optional Robotic Public and Consumer Safety Protocol
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Advanced automation can increase productive output and economic rent while weakening the historic connection between production, labour income, household demand and the domestic tax base. This working paper develops an institutional response for the post-post-automation economy through two separately adoptable instruments. Part I proposes the International Automation Rent and Destination Equalisation Accord (IARDEA). Rather than treating relocation as the taxable event or imposing a conventional border tariff, the framework establishes an enterprise-level Destination Equalisation Tax (DET). A 24 per cent ordinary company-tax benchmark is combined, as an explicit calibration parameter, with a 16 per cent excess-rent layer. Excess rent is identified at consolidated-group level before destination allocation, reducing the ability of internal royalties, intellectual-property migration and related-party financing to relocate the rent through accounting form alone. Equivalent foreign taxes are credited to prevent double collection. The framework adds an Essential Import Consumer-Incidence Cap (ECIC), deferred equalisation balances, distributor anti-squeeze safeguards, commercial-substance safe harbours, structured rebuttal and document-request procedures, constituent-State compliance rules for economic blocs, mutual recognition, information exchange, and non-retaliatory dispute settlement. Part II develops a separately adoptable Robotic Public and Consumer Safety Protocol for the continuing obligations created by autonomous productive capital. It covers continuing safety warranties, Robot-as-a-Service maintenance and replacement, accountable human oversight, foreseeable public interference, incident response, software-version responsibility, secure staged updates, event-record preservation, multi-robot incidents, end-of-support duties, no safety-by-subscription, and financial continuity where a provider fails. The paper includes preliminary EU/WTO and international-tax compatibility analysis, a Group Adjusted Capital schedule, Pillar Two interaction rules, ECIC and distributor worked examples, and synthetic stress tests examining intellectual-property migration and avoidance pathways. The central proposition is that a post-automation settlement requires more than replacing lost household income. It also requires mechanisms for maintaining the public claim on highly automated productive capacity, protecting economic circulation from incidence shocks, and assigning continuing responsibilities to autonomous capital operating within human environments. Supplementary Annex A — Post-Publication Validation Notes (6 September 2026). A companion annex has subsequently been added to this record to document design questions, proposed refinements and validation tasks arising from post-publication critique. It does not amend or replace the published v0.3 working paper. The annex addresses origin-neutral treatment of non-Party foreign-tax credits; cross-sector incidence of the cost-basis Group Adjusted Capital (KGK_G) rule; proposed Controlled Group and de minimis thresholds; a proposed statutory Safe Service Life floor for robotic systems; Tier 2 multi-provider compensation backstops; coalition and entry-into-force fragmentation risks; revised interpretation of the first synthetic pilot; and legal and technical reference verification. These items are retained as prospective material for later validation and any future consolidated instrument. Two-Page Policy Brief — 6 September 2026. A concise policy brief has also been added to this record for readers who want the institutional architecture without the full treaty drafting. It summarises the economic problem, the IARDEA/DET mechanism, consumer-incidence protections, the optional Robotic Public and Consumer Safety Protocol, and the principal legal, empirical and institutional steps required for further development.

papers.title: MOPG-7: A Multi-Clinic Dental Panoramic Radiograph Dataset with Expert YOLO Labels
papers.venue: Mendeley Data
papers.abstract: This dataset is a publicly available, multi-clinic dental imaging database that aims at furthering studies on artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, and computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) based on panoramic dental radiographs (orthopantomogram or OPG). This database includes 2,095 completely anonymized panoramic dental radiographs gathered retrospectively from four separate dental centers in Bangladesh, namely Sonia Nursing Home, Tangail (1,433 radiographs); Ibn Sina D. Lab & Consultation Center, Dayaganj (533 radiographs); Niramoy Diagnostic Center, Tangail (114 radiographs); and Health City Diagnostic Center, Gaibandha (15 radiographs). Every image comes with bounding box annotations in both YOLO (.txt) and standard COCO JSON format, validated by experts, making the dataset easy to use with frameworks such as Ultralytics YOLO as well as any COCO-compatible model or data loader. Initial bounding boxes were drawn by a licensed dentist and independently reviewed by a second dental professional. A rigorous quality-control process followed, removing 127 substandard bounding boxes, resulting in 9,834 validated bounding boxes. Dataset Classes The dataset includes annotations for seven clinically relevant dental categories: - Missing Teeth: 2,609 annotations - Dental Crown: 1,984 annotations - Root Canal: 1,956 annotations - Caries: 1,410 annotations - Wisdom Teeth: 869 annotations - Broken Down Teeth: 795 annotations - Healthy OPG: 211 annotations Dataset Contents The released dataset includes: - Panoramic dental radiographs (.jpg) - COCO-format JSON annotation files (instances_train.json, instances_val.json, instances_test.json) - YOLO bounding-box annotation files (.txt) - Metadata files (class_definitions.csv, image_metadata.csv, split_assignments.csv) - Documentation (README.md) describing the dataset structure, annotation format, and usage instructions Potential Research Applications This dataset supports multi-class dental object detection, localization of dental abnormalities, CAD, deep learning for medical imaging, computer vision research, transfer learning and foundation models, explainable AI (XAI), medical image analysis, object detection benchmarking, AI-enabled dental diagnosis, dental AI learning, and reproducibility research. Benchmark Performance Three YOLO variants were evaluated to establish a baseline. YOLOv8m achieved the highest precision (71.9%) and mAP@0.5 (72.9%), with the fastest inference latency (1.9 ms per radiograph). YOLOv10m achieved the highest recall (74.2%) and mAP@0.5:0.95 (34.4%), with a latency of 3.4 ms. YOLOv11m reached a precision of 70.9%, recall of 71.6%, mAP@0.5 of 71.7%, and mAP@0.5:0.95 of 33.5%, with a latency of 4.2 ms. These results show the comparative detection performance and computational efficiency of the evaluated YOLO variants on this dataset.

papers.title: "Phishing Screenshots Dataset"
papers.venue: IEEE DataPort
papers.abstract: "This dataset was developed as part of a cybersecurity research initiative focused on detecting phishing attacks through visual analysis of webpage screenshots. It contains approximately 2,759 unique labeled screenshot images with 4,935 detailed visual, structural, and content-based features. The dataset includes 1,316 legitimate webpage screenshots and 1,443 phishing webpage screenshots. Features include deep spatial representations extracted using EfficientNetB3, along with handcrafted forensic features such as Error Level Analysis (ELA) variance, GLCM texture descriptors, and color-space statistical moments. The dataset supports research in machine learning, computer vision, web security, and phishing detection, enabling models to distinguish between legitimate and phishing webpages based on visual characteristics. It can be used for visual phishing detection, browser security, explainable AI, multimodal threat intelligence, adversarial robustness testing, and cybersecurity education."

papers.title: 超空间几何的动态拓扑转换与几何优化
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology transformation algorithm based on the concept of super-space geometry, designed to automate geometric transformations with robust quality and stability. The algorithm leverages the inherent properties of super-space geometry – its continuity, stability, and ability to represent complex transformations – to facilitate intelligent and automated geometric optimization. We present a framework for generating and optimizing geometric transformations through a dynamic process, incorporating geometric optimization techniques to enhance transformation quality. The core mechanism hinges on a continuous and stable transformation driven by a dynamic optimization loop. This approach offers a significant advancement over traditional methods, particularly in the context of visual geometry and computer vision, where automated and high-quality transformations are crucial. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results, demonstrating its potential for generating and optimizing geometric shapes with enhanced quality and stability.

papers.title: Title: Non-Linear Matrix Completion with Adaptive Bias
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Non-linear matrix completion remains a significant challenge in various fields, including image processing, computer vision, and data analysis. Traditional methods often struggle with data that exhibits complex nonlinear relationships, demanding computationally intensive and potentially suboptimal solutions. This paper introduces a novel non-linear matrix completion method, termed "Bias-Adaptive" completion, that addresses these limitations by dynamically adjusting a bias term based on the matrix's intrinsic properties and the data it represents. The core mechanism hinges on a sophisticated learning algorithm that establishes a representation of the matrix's structure, enabling the algorithm to intelligently refine the bias to maximize the likelihood of successful completion. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on a diverse dataset of non-linear matrices, showcasing its superior performance compared to existing techniques. The paper explores the underlying principles of the algorithm, highlights the benefits of adaptive bias, and provides a detailed analysis of the methodology. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of this method in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: The Use of Eye-Tracking Technology in Research on Psychotherapists and Clinicians: A PRISMA-ScR Scoping Review.
papers.venue: Open Science Framework
papers.abstract: This review of the research literature focuses on the use of eye-tracking technology and computer vision to objectively measure the visual behavior of healthcare professionals—including physicians and mental health specialists—during clinical encounters and supervision sessions. Although nonverbal communication and mutual eye contact are fundamental to the therapeutic alliance and clinical empathy, the objective quantification of a healthcare professional’s gaze remains under-researched. The main objective of this project is to determine the scope, extent, and nature of empirical research utilizing hardware-based eye-tracking devices and AI-based visual algorithms (e.g., pose estimation, facial gaze analysis) to track the behavior of professionals in clinical and psychotherapeutic settings, with a clear exclusion of studies focusing exclusively on the patient. The methodology complies with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and utilizes the PCC (Population, Concept, Context) framework for a systematic search of major databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and PsycINFO). Expected results include: A comprehensive synthesis of currently available eye-tracking and computer vision technologies used in clinical and healthcare contexts. The identification of specific clinical phenomena (e.g., therapeutic alliance, countertransference, empathy) operationalized through gaze parameters. Highlighting current methodological gaps and technological limitations in the literature. Providing an evidence-based foundation for future empirical research and the development of innovative tools for clinical training, supervision, and teletherapy interfaces.

papers.title: Title: Non-Euclidean Object Recognition – Hierarchical Feature Extraction via Adaptive Graph Embeddings
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Object recognition has long been a challenging task in computer vision, with traditional methods often struggling to effectively capture the nuances of complex scenes. This research explores a novel approach to object recognition utilizing hierarchical feature extraction and adaptive graph embeddings. The core principle is to construct a graph representation of the image, where nodes represent features and edges represent relationships between these features. A dynamic graph structure is then generated based on the object's complexity, allowing the system to adapt to varying levels of detail. This system aims to overcome the limitations of current methods by providing a more robust and adaptable framework for object identification. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a series of experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing improved accuracy and adaptability compared to existing techniques.

papers.title: BLD-BD: A Field-Based Image Dataset of Bean Leaf Diseases for Deep Learning & Computer Vision Research
papers.venue: Mendeley Data
papers.abstract: Overview: This dataset contains high-resolution images of bean leaves collected directly from agricultural fields in Kulchara village, located in the Jhenaidah district of Bangladesh. It is specifically curated for computer vision tasks such as plant disease detection, classification, and deep learning model benchmarking (e.g., ResNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet). The dataset comprises three distinct classes: 1. Angular Leaf Spot 2. Bean Common Mosaic Virus 3. Healthy All images in both sub-datasets have been standardized to a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels in RGB format, ensuring clean background contrast and clear presentation of individual leaf disease symptoms. Dataset Structure & Content The dataset is divided into two separate compressed ZIP files: 1. Original_Bean_Leaf_Disease_Dataset.zip • Total Images: 672 original images • Distribution: Balanced across 3 classes (224 images per class) • Resolution: 512 × 512 pixels • Purpose: Serves as the raw, baseline field dataset for evaluation and baseline model benchmarking. 2. Augmented_Bean_Leaf_Disease_Dataset.zip • Total Images: 3,360 images • Distribution: 1,120 images per class (224 original + 896 augmented images) • Resolution: 512 × 512 pixels • Augmentation Techniques Applied: Controlled rotation (±15°), horizontal flipping, subtle random zoom/crop (5 - 10%), light exposure/brightness adjustments, and minimal Gaussian blur. • Note: Color signatures (hue/saturation) were strictly preserved to maintain the visual integrity of brown spots and green mosaic patterns vital for classification. Data Collection & Methodology The primary image acquisition was conducted under natural environmental lighting conditions in the field to reflect real-world agricultural scenarios. Data preprocessing included strict filtering to remove noisy background artifacts and non-target plant species. • Location of Collection: Village: Kulchara, District: Jhenaidah, Bangladesh • File Format: .jpg Potential Applications • Computer Vision and Agricultural AI Research • Single-label Leaf Disease Classification • Transfer Learning and Hybrid Deep Learning Model Training • Comparative Performance Analysis of CNN and Vision Transformer Models

papers.title: Multi-Scale Physical Information Fusion Algorithm
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
topics: Distributed Sensor Networks and Detection Algorithms
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel multi-scale physical information fusion algorithm designed to enhance accuracy and robustness in computer vision and sensor fusion tasks. The core concept revolves around recognizing and leveraging the inherent relationships between physical information at different scales. The algorithm employs a multi-resolution analysis technique to map data from diverse sensors—including images, radar, and sonar—onto corresponding physical scales. Subsequently, an optimization algorithm is utilized to fuse these multi-scale representations, achieving superior performance compared to traditional, single-scale fusion methods. The key innovation lies in explicitly addressing the correlations between data originating from different scales, overcoming the limitations of conventional sensor fusion approaches. The proposed method offers a flexible framework for integrating heterogeneous data streams, making it suitable for a wide range of applications where multi-scale contextual understanding is crucial. Experimental results, though not presented here, demonstrate significant improvements in various fusion metrics.

papers.title: Silkworm_Diseases_Dataset
papers.venue: Mendeley Data
papers.abstract: Total Images: 5,529 Disease/Health Classes: Healthy, Pebrine, Grasserie,Flacherie Target: Overlapping silkworms,Healthy, Pebrine, Grasserie, Flacherie Applications: Disease classification, object detection, instance segmentation, silkworm counting, and health monitoring. This dataset contains images of silkworms categorized into five classes: Flacherie, Grasserie, Healthy Silkworm, Overlap, and Pebrine. The images are organized into training, testing, and split subsets to support machine-learning-based silkworm disease classification. The dataset is intended for research and development of computer vision and deep learning models for automated silkworm disease identification.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Monitoring and Sustainable Development
papers.venue: OpenAlex
papers.abstract: This paper explores the role of AI in environmental monitoring and sustainable development, with specific emphasis on the Nigerian context. Using systems theory as the conceptual framework, the study highlights the diverse applications of AI, including remote sensing, air and water quality assessment, waste management, biodiversity conservation, and disaster risk prediction. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative tool in addressing the pressing challenges of environmental monitoring and sustainable development. By leveraging advanced machine learning algorithms, computer vision, and data analytics, AI enables efficient collection, processing, and interpretation of large-scale environmental data. Applications span across climate modelling, air and water quality assessment, biodiversity conservation, precision agriculture, renewable energy optimisation, and disaster risk management. AI-powered systems enhance the accuracy of predictions, support real-time monitoring, and facilitate informed decision-making for policymakers and stakeholders. Despite its vast potential, challenges such as data privacy, high energy consumption, technological inequality, and ethical considerations remain critical concerns. Integrating AI into environmental management requires collaborative frameworks that balance technological innovation with ecological and social responsibility. Furthermore, the paper examines how AI contributes to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goals 6, 7, 11, and 13, fostering resilient ecosystems and promoting a greener, more sustainable future.

papers.title: Computer Vision and Artificial Intelligence-Driven Structural Health Monitoring in Water Conservancy: Intelligent Early Warning and Economic Benefit Optimization
papers.venue: Asia Pacific Economic and Management Review
papers.abstract: Water conservancy structures serve as the core infrastructure for the operation of water conservancy projects; their structural health directly impacts regional flood control safety, water resource supply security, and ecological environment safety. Traditional health monitoring of water conservancy structures relies on manual inspections and wired sensing devices, but this approach suffers from limitations such as limited coverage, insufficient detection timeliness, and high maintenance and operation costs. This paper investigates the application of computer vision and artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in the field of water conservancy structure health monitoring. It outlines the technical pathways employed by computer vision techniques to identify structural anomalies—such as surface cracks, deformation, or damage—and analyzes the predictive logic of AI algorithms for forecasting the evolution trends of structural health. The paper proposes a framework for an intelligent safety early-warning system tailored for water conservancy structures and systematically evaluates the economic benefits derived from the application of these technologies from both direct and indirect perspectives. Case studies based on actual engineering applications demonstrate that this technical framework can significantly enhance the accuracy of anomaly detection and the timeliness of early warnings for water conservancy structures, reduce manual maintenance and operation costs, and extend the service life of these structures. Finally, this paper identifies the challenges currently faced during the implementation phase of these technologies—particularly in data processing and privacy protection—and proposes corresponding solutions. It also offers insights into future technological development directions in this field, providing a valuable reference for the intelligent operation and maintenance of water conservancy projects.

papers.title: Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding for 3D Data
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has achieved remarkable success in computer vision, but its application to 3D data remains limited. Traditional SSL approaches often fail to capture the inherent hierarchical structure present in 3D representations like point clouds and meshes. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical self-supervised learning framework that addresses this challenge. Our approach combines a hierarchical architecture with contrastive predictive coding (CPC) to learn robust and meaningful 3D representations. The core idea is to progressively refine representations, starting from coarse predictions at lower levels and progressively incorporating contrastive learning to ensure consistency across hierarchical levels. We formulate the learning process as a series of predictions and contrastive losses, leading to a richer and more structurally aware representation of the input 3D data. The resulting representation is suitable for downstream tasks such as 3D object recognition, segmentation, and retrieval. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through theoretical analysis and a comprehensive evaluation on benchmark 3D datasets.

papers.title: From Paper Manifests to Real-Time GPS: The Fascinating Evolution of Package Tracking Technology
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Not that long ago, buying something from a mail-order catalog or an early online storefront was an exercise in pure patience. You submitted your order, crossed your fingers, and waited out the standard disclaimer: “Please allow four to six weeks for delivery.” During those weeks, your item existed in a logistical black hole. You had no way to check its location, no estimated delivery date, and no recourse other than calling a customer service helpline if the parcel simply never arrived. Today, the landscape looks radically different. The moment an order confirmation hits your inbox, you expect instant, end-to-end visibility. We pull out our phones, check high-precision delivery maps, and receive ping notifications the exact second a box lands on our front porch. The transition from blind faith to minute-by-minute visibility is one of the most remarkable logistical and technological achievements of the digital age. Here is a look at how package tracking technology evolved from humble paper logs to the sophisticated, AI-driven global networks we rely on today. The Pre-Digital Era: Paper Waybills and Blind Transit Before microchips and digital networks, freight and postal services operated entirely on paper. Packages traveled alongside physical documents called waybills or cargo manifests. Dispatchers and dockworkers manually recorded item numbers, origins, and destinations on paper ledger sheets. If a merchant or customer wanted to locate a shipment, logistics clerks had to trace the paper trail by calling intermediate distribution hubs along the transit route via telephone or teletype. If a waybill went missing or got damaged by weather, the cargo effectively vanished into the system until someone physically discovered it at a sorting terminal. True shipment tracking in transit simply did not exist for everyday consumers. The Barcode Revolution (1970s–1980s) The first major leap toward modern tracking occurred in the late 1970s and early 1980s, spearheaded by the adoption of linear barcodes and computerized data networks. Industry pioneers realized that hand-recording serial numbers created bottlenecks and human error. During this era, logistics firms introduced optical barcode scanners and centralized tracking mainframes. When a parcel was sorted at an air hub or regional depot, a worker scanned its barcode using a handheld device or stationary conveyor scanner. This scan recorded a timestamp and a facility code, which was uploaded in batches to a central database. For the first time, logistics managers could review the history of where an item had been scanned. While this data was primarily used internally by operations teams to manage route capacity, it laid the foundational architecture for automated parcel tracking. The Web 1.0 Era: Bringing Tracking to the Consumer In the mid-1990s, the rise of the commercial World Wide Web changed consumer expectations forever. Instead of calling a 1-800 number to speak with a dispatcher, shippers began exploring ways to make scan data publicly accessible. In late 1994, FedEx launched the first website feature that allowed customers to enter a tracking code into an online form and see scan events on their own screens. UPS, DHL, and national postal operators quickly followed suit. Suddenly, entering a sequence of digits to track your package became a routine part of buying goods remotely. These early systems relied on batch-uploaded updates. Scanners synced with central servers every few hours via wired docks or dial-up modems. While not instantaneous, it gave buyers peace of mind and significantly reduced inbound support calls for retailers. Cellular Telematics, GPS, and Dynamic Scanning (2000s–2010s) As cellular networks transitioned from 2G to 3G and 4G, and GPS chips became small and affordable, logistics visibility shifted from stationary scans to dynamic, moving data streams. Mobile Computer Scanners Delivery drivers were equipped with ruggedized cellular terminals. Instead of saving scan data for the end-of-day dock return, these devices transmitted scan events in real time over cellular networks. The moment a courier scanned a parcel at your doorstep, the server updated. Fleet Telematics and Active GPS Freight companies began outfitting delivery vans, semi-trucks, and shipping containers with GPS telematics units. Dispatchers could see the precise geographical coordinates, speed, and heading of every vehicle in their fleet. This granular data enabled modern delivery tracking features, such as live route maps and narrow time-window estimates (“Your driver is 5 stops away”). The Cross-Border Boom and Universal Aggregators As global e-commerce expanded over the last decade, supply chains grew increasingly complex. A single online purchase might now be picked up by a local courier in Asia, flown internationally by a freight forwarder, cleared through customs, handed over to a national postal system, and ultimately delivered by a regional gig-economy driver. This multi-leg routing created a serious visibility problem: each carrier operated within its own proprietary software silo, forcing customers to juggle multiple tracking numbers across different languages and foreign websites. Relying on a single carrier tracking page often resulted in dead ends once a box crossed an international border. To solve this fragmentation, modern universal platforms emerged. Multi-carrier services like TrackPkgs aggregate tracking updates across more than 1,500 postal and courier networks worldwide. By automatically identifying the courier and stitching together tracking events from every leg of transit into a single feed, these tools ensure buyers and merchants maintain clear visibility regardless of how many handoffs occur along the journey. The Modern Frontier: IoT, AI, and Predictive Visibility Tracking technology is now entering an era powered by the Internet of Things (IoT) and machine learning. We are moving beyond tracking where an item is to understanding its condition and predicting its future: Environmental Sensor Tags: High-value shipments, such as pharmaceuticals and sensitive electronics, now travel with miniature IoT sensors that broadcast temperature, humidity, shock, tilt, and light exposure in real time. Predictive ETA Algorithms: Artificial intelligence models analyze historical traffic trends, weather forecasts, port congestion, and seasonal package volumes to predict delays before they happen and dynamically reroute shipments. Computer Vision and Proof of Delivery: Modern drivers use high-resolution cameras to capture geotagged, timestamped delivery photos, providing immediate visual verification that eliminates porch-piracy ambiguity. Looking Ahead From paper waybills passed hand-to-hand across train depots to satellite-linked telemetry and automated universal tracking systems, our ability to monitor physical goods across the globe has transformed completely. Today, transparency is not an added bonus—it is an essential pillar of global trade. As automated fulfillment centers, autonomous delivery vehicles, and smart sensor networks continue to mature, the future of shipment visibility promises to be faster, more precise, and more seamless than ever before.

papers.title: Title: Cognitive-Computational Geometry – Modeling Human Spatial Reasoning
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper explores the intersection of cognitive science and geometric modeling through the development of a computational model designed to simulate human spatial reasoning. The core claim is to create a machine learning-driven system capable of generating realistic geometric simulations directly mirroring the neural processes underpinning spatial cognition. We propose a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture, trained on datasets of human spatial perception, to learn and emulate these patterns. This endeavor aims to provide a foundational platform for advanced computer vision, robotics, and spatial navigation systems by directly modeling the underlying cognitive mechanisms. The potential impact of this research lies in fostering a more intuitive and effective representation of spatial understanding within artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Relational Databases via Query Generation
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has achieved remarkable success in areas like computer vision and natural language processing. However, its application to relational databases remains largely unexplored due to the absence of readily available, labeled data. This paper proposes a novel approach to self-supervised learning for relational databases by leveraging query generation. We train a neural network to generate SQL queries from the database schema and its data. These generated queries serve as pseudo-labels, enabling the network to learn effective relational representations without relying on manual annotation. Our method capitalizes on the inherent structure of relational data, offering a promising pathway for building robust and adaptable database systems through SSL. The core idea is to transform a supervised problem (query answering) into an unsupervised one (query generation), allowing the model to learn representations based on the relationships within the data. This approach avoids the bottleneck of needing labeled query-answer pairs. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and outline potential future research directions.

papers.title: BLD-BD: A Field-Based Image Dataset of Bean Leaf Diseases for Deep Learning & Computer Vision Research
papers.venue: Mendeley Data
papers.abstract: Overview: This dataset contains high-resolution images of bean leaves collected directly from agricultural fields in Kulchara village, located in the Jhenaidah district of Bangladesh. It is specifically curated for computer vision tasks such as plant disease detection, classification, and deep learning model benchmarking (e.g., ResNet, MobileNet, EfficientNet). The dataset comprises three distinct classes: 1. Angular Leaf Spot 2. Bean Common Mosaic Virus 3. Healthy All images in both sub-datasets have been standardized to a resolution of 512 × 512 pixels in RGB format, ensuring clean background contrast and clear presentation of individual leaf disease symptoms. Dataset Structure & Content The dataset is divided into two separate compressed ZIP files: 1. Original_Bean_Leaf_Disease_Dataset.zip • Total Images: 672 original images • Distribution: Balanced across 3 classes (224 images per class) • Resolution: 512 × 512 pixels • Purpose: Serves as the raw, baseline field dataset for evaluation and baseline model benchmarking. 2. Augmented_Bean_Leaf_Disease_Dataset.zip • Total Images: 3,360 images • Distribution: 1,120 images per class (224 original + 896 augmented images) • Resolution: 512 × 512 pixels • Augmentation Techniques Applied: Controlled rotation (±15°), horizontal flipping, subtle random zoom/crop (5 - 10%), light exposure/brightness adjustments, and minimal Gaussian blur. • Note: Color signatures (hue/saturation) were strictly preserved to maintain the visual integrity of brown spots and green mosaic patterns vital for classification. Data Collection & Methodology The primary image acquisition was conducted under natural environmental lighting conditions in the field to reflect real-world agricultural scenarios. Data preprocessing included strict filtering to remove noisy background artifacts and non-target plant species. • Location of Collection: Village: Kulchara, District: Jhenaidah, Bangladesh • File Format: .jpg Potential Applications • Computer Vision and Agricultural AI Research • Single-label Leaf Disease Classification • Transfer Learning and Hybrid Deep Learning Model Training • Comparative Performance Analysis of CNN and Vision Transformer Models

papers.title: An Integrated AI Automating Inspection Model for Surface Defect Segmentation and Classification in Construction Domain
papers.venue: Journal of Intelligent Computing System
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection
papers.abstract: Unlike stone age, humans no longer live in caves or mud houses but rather shifted to modern civilization setups which include - buildings, bridges and industrial facilities as their environment. And with time these structures and components develop surface defects like cracks, peeling, spalling, algae, staining and manufacturing flaws. If frequently, these structures are left untreated, then it may affect human safety and threaten serviceability. For inspection purposes, only relying on manual visual examination will lead to a slow process and some parts may be left unchecked. This will add pressure on pockets. Moreover, this method is slow, subjective, costly, error-prone and unsafe for surfaces which are inaccessible. Overall, these factors motivate automated computer vision inspection. However, there exists some constraints like limited, imbalanced datasets and inspection spans of various distinct types of tasks. This work gives unified Deep Learning model which evaluates on one of the public benchmark datasets from Kaggle which consists of sub folders of Magnetic-Tile Defect, DeepPCB, DBCC bridge cracks and CrackForest. In this paper multi-class classification, binary classification and pixel-level segmentation are considered. The model couple’s residual backbone with classification, which is regularized head and symmetric U-Net. Overall is trained from scratch without pre-training and employs objective which is imbalanced (class-weighted, positive weighted BCE with Dice, label-smoothed cross entropy). This framework attains F1 score of 0.9945 for DeepPCB dataset. The novelty lies in its approach, as its single, pre-training free pipeline which spans three task paradigms with the issue of handling imbalance and format agnostic ingestion and in real honest finding that scale of data, more than architecture and govern effectiveness. Future work could focus on adding pre- trained backbones, multi-seed evaluation and board- disjoint and then end to end detection.
