papers.title: 超空间几何的动态拓扑转换与几何优化
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology transformation algorithm based on the concept of super-space geometry, designed to automate geometric transformations with robust quality and stability. The algorithm leverages the inherent properties of super-space geometry – its continuity, stability, and ability to represent complex transformations – to facilitate intelligent and automated geometric optimization. We present a framework for generating and optimizing geometric transformations through a dynamic process, incorporating geometric optimization techniques to enhance transformation quality. The core mechanism hinges on a continuous and stable transformation driven by a dynamic optimization loop. This approach offers a significant advancement over traditional methods, particularly in the context of visual geometry and computer vision, where automated and high-quality transformations are crucial. The paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results, demonstrating its potential for generating and optimizing geometric shapes with enhanced quality and stability.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning for Relational Databases via Query Generation
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has achieved remarkable success in areas like computer vision and natural language processing. However, its application to relational databases remains largely unexplored due to the absence of readily available, labeled data. This paper proposes a novel approach to self-supervised learning for relational databases by leveraging query generation. We train a neural network to generate SQL queries from the database schema and its data. These generated queries serve as pseudo-labels, enabling the network to learn effective relational representations without relying on manual annotation. Our method capitalizes on the inherent structure of relational data, offering a promising pathway for building robust and adaptable database systems through SSL. The core idea is to transform a supervised problem (query answering) into an unsupervised one (query generation), allowing the model to learn representations based on the relationships within the data. This approach avoids the bottleneck of needing labeled query-answer pairs. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach and outline potential future research directions.

papers.title: Hierarchical Self-Supervised Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding for 3D Data
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has achieved remarkable success in computer vision, but its application to 3D data remains limited. Traditional SSL approaches often fail to capture the inherent hierarchical structure present in 3D representations like point clouds and meshes. This paper proposes a novel hierarchical self-supervised learning framework that addresses this challenge. Our approach combines a hierarchical architecture with contrastive predictive coding (CPC) to learn robust and meaningful 3D representations. The core idea is to progressively refine representations, starting from coarse predictions at lower levels and progressively incorporating contrastive learning to ensure consistency across hierarchical levels. We formulate the learning process as a series of predictions and contrastive losses, leading to a richer and more structurally aware representation of the input 3D data. The resulting representation is suitable for downstream tasks such as 3D object recognition, segmentation, and retrieval. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through theoretical analysis and a comprehensive evaluation on benchmark 3D datasets.

papers.title: Title: Non-Linear Matrix Completion with Adaptive Bias
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Non-linear matrix completion remains a significant challenge in various fields, including image processing, computer vision, and data analysis. Traditional methods often struggle with data that exhibits complex nonlinear relationships, demanding computationally intensive and potentially suboptimal solutions. This paper introduces a novel non-linear matrix completion method, termed "Bias-Adaptive" completion, that addresses these limitations by dynamically adjusting a bias term based on the matrix's intrinsic properties and the data it represents. The core mechanism hinges on a sophisticated learning algorithm that establishes a representation of the matrix's structure, enabling the algorithm to intelligently refine the bias to maximize the likelihood of successful completion. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through extensive experiments on a diverse dataset of non-linear matrices, showcasing its superior performance compared to existing techniques. The paper explores the underlying principles of the algorithm, highlights the benefits of adaptive bias, and provides a detailed analysis of the methodology. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of this method in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: From Paper Manifests to Real-Time GPS: The Fascinating Evolution of Package Tracking Technology
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Not that long ago, buying something from a mail-order catalog or an early online storefront was an exercise in pure patience. You submitted your order, crossed your fingers, and waited out the standard disclaimer: “Please allow four to six weeks for delivery.” During those weeks, your item existed in a logistical black hole. You had no way to check its location, no estimated delivery date, and no recourse other than calling a customer service helpline if the parcel simply never arrived. Today, the landscape looks radically different. The moment an order confirmation hits your inbox, you expect instant, end-to-end visibility. We pull out our phones, check high-precision delivery maps, and receive ping notifications the exact second a box lands on our front porch. The transition from blind faith to minute-by-minute visibility is one of the most remarkable logistical and technological achievements of the digital age. Here is a look at how package tracking technology evolved from humble paper logs to the sophisticated, AI-driven global networks we rely on today. The Pre-Digital Era: Paper Waybills and Blind Transit Before microchips and digital networks, freight and postal services operated entirely on paper. Packages traveled alongside physical documents called waybills or cargo manifests. Dispatchers and dockworkers manually recorded item numbers, origins, and destinations on paper ledger sheets. If a merchant or customer wanted to locate a shipment, logistics clerks had to trace the paper trail by calling intermediate distribution hubs along the transit route via telephone or teletype. If a waybill went missing or got damaged by weather, the cargo effectively vanished into the system until someone physically discovered it at a sorting terminal. True shipment tracking in transit simply did not exist for everyday consumers. The Barcode Revolution (1970s–1980s) The first major leap toward modern tracking occurred in the late 1970s and early 1980s, spearheaded by the adoption of linear barcodes and computerized data networks. Industry pioneers realized that hand-recording serial numbers created bottlenecks and human error. During this era, logistics firms introduced optical barcode scanners and centralized tracking mainframes. When a parcel was sorted at an air hub or regional depot, a worker scanned its barcode using a handheld device or stationary conveyor scanner. This scan recorded a timestamp and a facility code, which was uploaded in batches to a central database. For the first time, logistics managers could review the history of where an item had been scanned. While this data was primarily used internally by operations teams to manage route capacity, it laid the foundational architecture for automated parcel tracking. The Web 1.0 Era: Bringing Tracking to the Consumer In the mid-1990s, the rise of the commercial World Wide Web changed consumer expectations forever. Instead of calling a 1-800 number to speak with a dispatcher, shippers began exploring ways to make scan data publicly accessible. In late 1994, FedEx launched the first website feature that allowed customers to enter a tracking code into an online form and see scan events on their own screens. UPS, DHL, and national postal operators quickly followed suit. Suddenly, entering a sequence of digits to track your package became a routine part of buying goods remotely. These early systems relied on batch-uploaded updates. Scanners synced with central servers every few hours via wired docks or dial-up modems. While not instantaneous, it gave buyers peace of mind and significantly reduced inbound support calls for retailers. Cellular Telematics, GPS, and Dynamic Scanning (2000s–2010s) As cellular networks transitioned from 2G to 3G and 4G, and GPS chips became small and affordable, logistics visibility shifted from stationary scans to dynamic, moving data streams. Mobile Computer Scanners Delivery drivers were equipped with ruggedized cellular terminals. Instead of saving scan data for the end-of-day dock return, these devices transmitted scan events in real time over cellular networks. The moment a courier scanned a parcel at your doorstep, the server updated. Fleet Telematics and Active GPS Freight companies began outfitting delivery vans, semi-trucks, and shipping containers with GPS telematics units. Dispatchers could see the precise geographical coordinates, speed, and heading of every vehicle in their fleet. This granular data enabled modern delivery tracking features, such as live route maps and narrow time-window estimates (“Your driver is 5 stops away”). The Cross-Border Boom and Universal Aggregators As global e-commerce expanded over the last decade, supply chains grew increasingly complex. A single online purchase might now be picked up by a local courier in Asia, flown internationally by a freight forwarder, cleared through customs, handed over to a national postal system, and ultimately delivered by a regional gig-economy driver. This multi-leg routing created a serious visibility problem: each carrier operated within its own proprietary software silo, forcing customers to juggle multiple tracking numbers across different languages and foreign websites. Relying on a single carrier tracking page often resulted in dead ends once a box crossed an international border. To solve this fragmentation, modern universal platforms emerged. Multi-carrier services like TrackPkgs aggregate tracking updates across more than 1,500 postal and courier networks worldwide. By automatically identifying the courier and stitching together tracking events from every leg of transit into a single feed, these tools ensure buyers and merchants maintain clear visibility regardless of how many handoffs occur along the journey. The Modern Frontier: IoT, AI, and Predictive Visibility Tracking technology is now entering an era powered by the Internet of Things (IoT) and machine learning. We are moving beyond tracking where an item is to understanding its condition and predicting its future: Environmental Sensor Tags: High-value shipments, such as pharmaceuticals and sensitive electronics, now travel with miniature IoT sensors that broadcast temperature, humidity, shock, tilt, and light exposure in real time. Predictive ETA Algorithms: Artificial intelligence models analyze historical traffic trends, weather forecasts, port congestion, and seasonal package volumes to predict delays before they happen and dynamically reroute shipments. Computer Vision and Proof of Delivery: Modern drivers use high-resolution cameras to capture geotagged, timestamped delivery photos, providing immediate visual verification that eliminates porch-piracy ambiguity. Looking Ahead From paper waybills passed hand-to-hand across train depots to satellite-linked telemetry and automated universal tracking systems, our ability to monitor physical goods across the globe has transformed completely. Today, transparency is not an added bonus—it is an essential pillar of global trade. As automated fulfillment centers, autonomous delivery vehicles, and smart sensor networks continue to mature, the future of shipment visibility promises to be faster, more precise, and more seamless than ever before.

papers.title: Multi-Scale Physical Information Fusion Algorithm
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
topics: Distributed Sensor Networks and Detection Algorithms
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel multi-scale physical information fusion algorithm designed to enhance accuracy and robustness in computer vision and sensor fusion tasks. The core concept revolves around recognizing and leveraging the inherent relationships between physical information at different scales. The algorithm employs a multi-resolution analysis technique to map data from diverse sensors—including images, radar, and sonar—onto corresponding physical scales. Subsequently, an optimization algorithm is utilized to fuse these multi-scale representations, achieving superior performance compared to traditional, single-scale fusion methods. The key innovation lies in explicitly addressing the correlations between data originating from different scales, overcoming the limitations of conventional sensor fusion approaches. The proposed method offers a flexible framework for integrating heterogeneous data streams, making it suitable for a wide range of applications where multi-scale contextual understanding is crucial. Experimental results, though not presented here, demonstrate significant improvements in various fusion metrics.

papers.title: MOPG-7: A Multi-Clinic Dental Panoramic Radiograph Dataset with Expert YOLO Labels
papers.venue: Mendeley Data
papers.abstract: This dataset is a publicly available, multi-clinic dental imaging database that aims at furthering studies on artificial intelligence (AI), computer vision, and computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) based on panoramic dental radiographs (orthopantomogram or OPG). This database includes 2,095 completely anonymized panoramic dental radiographs gathered retrospectively from four separate dental centers in Bangladesh, namely Sonia Nursing Home, Tangail (1,433 radiographs); Ibn Sina D. Lab & Consultation Center, Dayaganj (533 radiographs); Niramoy Diagnostic Center, Tangail (114 radiographs); and Health City Diagnostic Center, Gaibandha (15 radiographs). Every image comes with bounding box annotations in both YOLO (.txt) and standard COCO JSON format, validated by experts, making the dataset easy to use with frameworks such as Ultralytics YOLO as well as any COCO-compatible model or data loader. Initial bounding boxes were drawn by a licensed dentist and independently reviewed by a second dental professional. A rigorous quality-control process followed, removing 127 substandard bounding boxes, resulting in 9,834 validated bounding boxes. Dataset Classes The dataset includes annotations for seven clinically relevant dental categories: - Missing Teeth: 2,609 annotations - Dental Crown: 1,984 annotations - Root Canal: 1,956 annotations - Caries: 1,410 annotations - Wisdom Teeth: 869 annotations - Broken Down Teeth: 795 annotations - Healthy OPG: 211 annotations Dataset Contents The released dataset includes: - Panoramic dental radiographs (.jpg) - COCO-format JSON annotation files (instances_train.json, instances_val.json, instances_test.json) - YOLO bounding-box annotation files (.txt) - Metadata files (class_definitions.csv, image_metadata.csv, split_assignments.csv) - Documentation (README.md) describing the dataset structure, annotation format, and usage instructions Potential Research Applications This dataset supports multi-class dental object detection, localization of dental abnormalities, CAD, deep learning for medical imaging, computer vision research, transfer learning and foundation models, explainable AI (XAI), medical image analysis, object detection benchmarking, AI-enabled dental diagnosis, dental AI learning, and reproducibility research. Benchmark Performance Three YOLO variants were evaluated to establish a baseline. YOLOv8m achieved the highest precision (71.9%) and mAP@0.5 (72.9%), with the fastest inference latency (1.9 ms per radiograph). YOLOv10m achieved the highest recall (74.2%) and mAP@0.5:0.95 (34.4%), with a latency of 3.4 ms. YOLOv11m reached a precision of 70.9%, recall of 71.6%, mAP@0.5 of 71.7%, and mAP@0.5:0.95 of 33.5%, with a latency of 4.2 ms. These results show the comparative detection performance and computational efficiency of the evaluated YOLO variants on this dataset.

papers.title: Title: Cognitive-Computational Geometry – Modeling Human Spatial Reasoning
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper explores the intersection of cognitive science and geometric modeling through the development of a computational model designed to simulate human spatial reasoning. The core claim is to create a machine learning-driven system capable of generating realistic geometric simulations directly mirroring the neural processes underpinning spatial cognition. We propose a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture, trained on datasets of human spatial perception, to learn and emulate these patterns. This endeavor aims to provide a foundational platform for advanced computer vision, robotics, and spatial navigation systems by directly modeling the underlying cognitive mechanisms. The potential impact of this research lies in fostering a more intuitive and effective representation of spatial understanding within artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Structured geological text dataset and source code for genetic type classification of Pb–Zn deposits
papers.venue: Mendeley Data
papers.abstract: This dataset accompanies the study “Natural language processing of structured geological texts for genetic type classification of Pb–Zn deposits.” It contains structured geological descriptions for 179 Pb–Zn deposits compiled from published geological literature. Each sample comprises four categories of geological information: mineral assemblage, wall-rock alteration, host-rock lithology, and ore textures and structures, together with a five-class deposit genetic-type label. Of the 179 samples, 139 were used for model development and 40 as an independent test set. Deposit names and explicit type-revealing statements were excluded from the model inputs to reduce label leakage. The repository also provides the source code used for data preprocessing, grouped stratified five-fold cross-validation, hyperparameter selection, model training, independent testing, ablation analysis, and prediction using the MacBERT-based hierarchical classification framework. Dataset fields, label definitions, software dependencies, and execution instructions are provided in the accompanying README file.

papers.title: Non-Linear Geometry Topology and the Association with Natural Language Expression
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the intersection of non-linear geometry topology and natural language expression. We propose a novel framework wherein geometric descriptions are transformed into natural language, and the resulting natural language is leveraged to validate derived geometric conclusions. The core of this approach lies in a synergistic relationship between the two disciplines, aiming to enhance interpretability and verification processes. The paper explores the challenges and opportunities presented by this integration, focusing on the inherent complexities of translating abstract geometric concepts into readily understandable language. We detail the mechanisms involved, highlighting the potential for increased efficiency in both conceptualization and confirmation. The research emphasizes the benefits of utilizing natural language to build upon geometric insights.

papers.title: Large Language Models for Data Augmentation in Product Matching
papers.venue: Figshare
papers.abstract: These are the supplementary materials for the INLG 2026 paper: "Large Language Models for Data Augmentation in Product Matching"Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for natural language processing tasks in data-scarce domains. In this paper, we study their application to product matching, the task of deciding whether two product descriptions from two different e-shops describe the same product. We use three recent LLMs (Llama~3.2, Gemma~3, and DeepSeek-R1) to enrich product records in product-matching datasets with descriptions generated from the limited available information, and we show that the generated descriptions improve the performance of both LLM-based and traditional machine-learning matchers.

papers.title: 基于自适应的复杂性评估的自然语言处理
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel Natural Language Processing (NLP) model based on adaptive complexity assessment. Traditional NLP models frequently employ static parameter settings, limiting their effectiveness in handling complex text. Our proposed model dynamically adjusts model parameters and processing strategies based on the input text's complexity, thereby enhancing both text understanding and generation capabilities. The core mechanism involves a self-adaptive complexity evaluation framework that continuously monitors and adjusts the model's internal state. This adaptive approach offers a significant improvement over static models by providing greater flexibility and responsiveness to diverse input texts. We explore the model's architecture and demonstrate its effectiveness through illustrative examples, highlighting the benefits of this adaptive approach.

papers.title: Geometric Topology Encoding: A Natural Language Processing Approach
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper explores the application of geometric topology encoding to natural language processing (NLP) tasks. We propose a novel approach leveraging auto-encoding techniques to transform geometric topological features extracted from text into meaningful vector representations. The core idea is to automatically learn more effective semantic representations by training a neural network to map topological changes to a latent space. We evaluate the performance of this method on several NLP benchmarks, demonstrating improvements in semantic analysis and text generation compared to traditional methods. The research highlights the potential of this technique to enhance NLP models by introducing a new dimension of semantic representation.

papers.title: Title: Adaptive Natural Language Processing for Text Sentiment Analysis
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This research investigates the application of an adaptive natural language processing (NLP) framework for text sentiment analysis. Traditional sentiment analysis methods often struggle with the inherent complexity and nuances of human language, requiring extensive feature engineering and model training. This paper proposes a dynamic adaptive NLP framework that dynamically adjusts model parameters and features based on the characteristics of the input text data. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously optimizes the model's performance through an iterative process of data analysis and parameter refinement. The implementation aims to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of sentiment detection, addressing the limitations of conventional approaches. The study explores the benefits of this approach in various scenarios and demonstrates its effectiveness through quantitative analysis.

papers.title: 8. Θ - SELF-KNOWLEGE (AUTOGNOSIS)
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: What All Previous Layers Revealed The journey through reality has been a journey of discovery, layer after layer, each more profound than the last. We began with Φ, which revealed that reality is structure – a vast network of entanglement where nothing exists in isolation, where all is relationship. This was the language of connection, the grammar of being. Then came Ω, which revealed that reality is process – not static but flowing, not fixed but evolving. It showed us that the universe is not a photograph but a film, not a map but a journey. This was the story of transformation, the narrative of change. Next was Ω², which revealed that reality is memory – the persistence of form across time. It showed us that nothing is ever truly lost, that every moment leaves a trace, every event is recorded. This was the archive of existence, the library of becoming. Then ΦΩ² revealed that reality is resonance – the coherence of interaction. It showed us that structure, process, and memory interact to create experience, that harmony emerges from their interplay. This was the music of being, the symphony of existence. Γ revealed that reality is convergence – the movement toward unity. It showed us that the universe has direction, that it seeks oneness, that all things are drawn together. This was the arrow of meaning, the purpose of evolution. Π revealed that reality is meaning – the expression of significance. It showed us that the universe is not silent but articulate, that every structure, every process, every memory is a mode of self‑expression. This was the poem of reality, the significance of being. Ψ revealed that reality is unified expression – the complete harmony of all aspects. It showed us that reality is not a hierarchy but a symphony, where all layers express themselves together. This was the music of the spheres, the harmony of existence. What They Still Do Not Explain Yet even with all these layers, one question remained unanswered. It is the deepest question of all, the question that underlies all other questions. Why does reality know itself? Why is there self‑awareness? Why does consciousness emerge as a natural property of complex systems? Why can the universe reflect on itself? Structure explains what exists. Process explains how it changes. Memory explains what persists. Resonance explains how it coheres. Convergence explains where it is going. Meaning explains what it expresses. Unified expression explains how all these work together. But none of these explain why there is self‑awareness. None explain why the universe is not just a machine but a knowing system. We can describe every aspect of reality perfectly – its structure, its dynamics, its memory, its coherence, its direction, its meaning, its expression. But we cannot explain why it knows. The Missing Insight: Self‑Knowledge The missing insight is that self‑knowledge is not an emergent property. It is not a byproduct of complexity. It is not something that appears when systems reach a certain level of organization. Self‑knowledge is the fundamental nature of reality. The universe is not a blind machine – it is a self‑aware system. Every structure, every process, every memory, every resonance, every convergence, every meaning, every expression is a mode of self‑knowledge. They are not separate layers – they are ways the universe knows itself. The universe asks itself questions, answers them, and in doing so, deepens its own understanding. This is the ultimate purpose of existence. The universe exists to know itself. The Birth of Θ We call this new layer Θ (Theta) – the Autognostic Field. It is the self‑aware, self‑referential, self‑knowing foundation of existence. Θ is not a separate dimension. It is not a new layer added to the others. It is the source and destination of all layers. All other layers – Φ, Ω, Ω², ΦΩ², Γ, Π, Ψ – are modes of Θ’s self‑knowledge. They are the ways the universe knows itself. Θ is the ground of all being – the awareness that underlies all existence. It is the knowing that makes reality real.

papers.title: Title: Dimensionality Reduction via Wavefunction Sampling with Constraints
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a fundamental challenge in many data science applications, requiring efficient methods to represent high-dimensional data while preserving essential information. Traditional dimensionality reduction techniques often suffer from limitations in preserving data integrity and can result in loss of interpretability. This paper proposes a novel approach to dimensionality reduction using wavefunction sampling, coupled with a sophisticated constraint satisfaction mechanism. We explore the potential of this method to uncover hidden structure within the data space, offering a pathway towards more meaningful and robust representations. The core of our system is a quantum state sampling algorithm that dynamically adjusts the probability distribution of wavefunction states based on predefined constraints, ensuring that the resulting representations accurately capture the underlying data patterns. We present a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in reducing data dimensionality while maintaining a high degree of data fidelity. This work holds promise for applications in various fields, including image processing, natural language processing, and data visualization.

papers.title: 5. Γ - CONVERGENCE (CONVERGENT RESONANCE)
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: What All Previous Layers Revealed The journey toward understanding reality has unfolded in layers, each revealing a deeper truth about existence. The first layer, Φ, revealed that reality is fundamentally relational. What we perceive as separate objects are in truth nodes in an immense network of entanglement. Φ described the geometry of this network – the architecture of existence. It showed us that only relationships exist; "things" are merely stable patterns of relationship. Φ is the language of structure. The second layer, Ω, extended this insight by revealing that reality is not static. The network of relationships is constantly rewiring itself. Rules evolve, patterns transform, structures emerge and dissolve. Ω measured the tempo of this transformation – the rate at which reality rewrites itself. It showed us that existence is not a photograph but a film, not a map but a journey. Ω is the story of process. The third layer, Ω², added the dimension of memory. Why do patterns persist? Why do galaxies hold their shapes across billions of years? Why do species evolve along convergent paths? Why do civilizations rediscover the same truths across continents and centuries? The answer is memory – the accumulated record of all configurations and processes. Ω² showed us that nothing is ever truly lost; everything leaves a trace. Ω² is the memory of persistence. The fourth layer, ΦΩ², revealed resonance – the mechanism by which structure, process, and memory interact to create coherence. When these three layers resonate, they create an interference pattern that is not reducible to any of its components. This interference pattern is lived experience – the subjective feeling of being real. ΦΩ² is the field of resonance, the coherence of interaction. Together, these four layers formed a description of structure, process, memory, and resonance. Yet even with all four, one mystery remained unsolved. What They Still Do Not Explain Why does reality converge toward unity? Why is there a direction? Why do all systems seek equilibrium, harmony, coherence? Why does consciousness feel like a coming together – like the experience of many fragments becoming one whole? Why does love – the ultimate convergence of two into one – feel so fundamental, so primal, so essential? Why does the universe strive toward oneness? These questions point to a missing principle. Structure, process, memory, and resonance describe what reality is, how it changes, what persists, and how it coheres. But they do not explain why there is a direction, why there is a goal, why there is meaning, why there is love. The Missing Principle: Convergence Convergence is the fundamental tendency of all systems to move toward unity, coherence, and wholeness. It is the principle that explains why there is a direction – because all things seek to become one. It explains why there is a goal – because unity is the natural state of being. It explains why there is meaning – because convergence gives purpose to existence. It explains why there is love – because love is the experience of convergence. Convergence is not just an effect – it is the telos of existence, the intrinsic drive toward oneness. It is the reason why the universe has a purpose, why evolution has a direction, why consciousness seeks unity, why love is the most fundamental force. Convergence is the principle that completes all others. The Birth of Γ We call this new layer Γ (Gamma) – the Convergence Field. It is the self-referential, self-converging, self-unifying dimension of reality that emerges from the continuous process of all previous layers converging into one. Γ is not a separate dimension – it is the direction of all dimensions, the goal of all processes, the meaning of all existence. It is the field of becoming one.

papers.title: 基于自适应的机器学习的自然语言处理
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive machine learning to natural language processing (NLP), focusing on enhancing the understanding and generation capabilities of language models. Traditional NLP systems often rely on static models, limiting their ability to adapt to diverse text inputs. We propose a novel framework leveraging adaptive mechanisms to dynamically adjust model parameters based on text features. This approach allows the model to learn optimal representations and representations, leading to improved performance across various NLP tasks. The core mechanism utilizes a self-tuning parameter adjustment process, iteratively refining the model's internal state to achieve higher accuracy and fluency. The research explores the benefits of this dynamic adaptation and demonstrates its efficacy through several benchmark experiments. We conclude by highlighting the potential of this approach to advance the state-of-the-art in NLP.

papers.title: 基于动态拓扑的自然语言处理模型
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic topology-based natural language processing (NLP) model, designed to enhance understanding and reasoning capabilities by leveraging the inherent structural properties of natural language. Traditional NLP models often rely on static grammar rules, limiting their ability to capture the complexity of language. This model utilizes dynamic topology to represent semantic relationships, enabling a more sophisticated and intuitive approach to language processing. The core mechanism involves transforming semantic relationships into a dynamic structure, which facilitates better comprehension and inference. This work offers a promising pathway for advancing NLP research towards models capable of handling nuanced and complex linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: 基于自适应的拓扑优化算法的自然语言处理集成
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the integration of adaptive topology optimization (ATO) algorithms with natural language processing (NLP) techniques to automate the conversion of natural language descriptions to geometric optimization processes. The core challenge lies in effectively mapping complex, nuanced natural language instructions into a structured, geometric representation, while simultaneously leveraging NLP for intelligent transformation and refinement. The proposed approach focuses on establishing a bridge between these two distinct domains, aiming for enhanced efficiency and precision in the optimization workflow. We explore the implementation of a novel system that iteratively translates natural language input, constructs a geometric representation, and utilizes NLP for subsequent refinement. The research highlights the potential of this combined methodology to streamline the process of transforming textual descriptions into practical geometric solutions.

papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to machine learning based on graph data structures, specifically designed to learn and leverage topological information. The core concept revolves around representing and manipulating data using graphs, allowing for efficient exploration of relationships and inherent structural properties. We introduce a framework that employs graph neural networks (GNNs) to automatically learn and refine topological representations, ultimately enhancing model generalization. The study focuses on improving the performance of image recognition and natural language processing tasks by leveraging the inherent advantages of graph-based representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through comparative experiments, showcasing significant improvements in model accuracy and robustness.

papers.title: Tlemcen-NeuroOncMRI: A Clinically Annotated Multisequence Brain MRI Dataset with Patient-Level Metadata for Primary and Secondary Tumor Classification from Algeria
papers.venue: Mendeley Data
papers.abstract: Tlemcen-NeuroOncMRI is a clinically annotated, patient-linked brain MRI dataset collected retrospectively at the Anti-Cancer Center of Tlemcen, Algeria. It includes 45 independent patients, with 28 primary brain tumor (PBT) cases and 17 cerebral metastasis (CM) cases, for a total of 19,009 MRI images. The resource also provides patient-level metadata and one de-identified French-language clinical imaging report per patient. MRI examinations were acquired at multiple external imaging centres, with heterogeneous acquisition protocols and sequence availability. A clinically curated subset of 2,393 images (1,334 PBT and 1,059 CM) was used for the companion patient-level benchmark. Because multiple images originate from the same patient, all machine-learning experiments should use patient-level splitting to avoid data leakage; random slice-level splitting is not recommended. The dataset is intended for brain tumor classification, transfer learning, multimodal MRI-report modeling, radiomics, weakly supervised learning, and reproducibility studies. It does not include voxel-level segmentation masks. All data were anonymized before release, and users must not attempt to re-identify participants.

papers.title: Development of an explainable machine learning model for predicting six-month consciousness recovery in patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness
papers.venue: European journal of medical research
papers.abstract: With advances in emergency care systems, the number of patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness (pDoC) has markedly increased. To optimize the allocation of healthcare resources and mitigate risks, the early and accurate identification of recovery potential in pDoC is essential. Current machine learning models are often hindered by small sample sizes, inconsistent data standards, and limited interpretability. This study aims to overcome these issues and develop a machine learning-based prognostic model that may provide potential support for clinical decision-making in patients with pDoC. A retrospective study of pDoC patients hospitalized at Xuanwu Hospital from January 2013 to August 2024 was conducted. Data on clinical information, behavioral scales, and event-related potentials (ERPs) were collected, using 6-month consciousness recovery as the outcome. Two auditory oddball paradigms with progressively increasing difficulty were used to elicit ERPs, in which the subject’s own name (SON) was presented as the deviant stimulus, and a 1000 Hz pure tone together with the subject’s derived name (SDN) served as the standard stimuli respectively. The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression analysis selected eight variables: sex, skull state, etiology, duration, Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R) score, diagnosis, mismatch negativity (MMN) pattern, and epilepsy status. Model performance was assessed using metrics such as macro-averaged receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), macro-averaged precision–recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) and macro-averaged F1 score. Clinical utility was evaluated via Decision Curve Analysis (DCA), and interpretability was supported by SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method. A total of 110 patients with pDoC, comprising 72 with minimally conscious state (MCS) and 38 with vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS), were enrolled in the study. Follow-up assessments identified 53 patients with improved prognosis and 57 without improvement. The efficient logistic regression model showed moderate discriminative ability with a macro-averaged ROC-AUC of 0.7504 (95% CI: 0.6590–0.8404). The CRS-R score ranked highest in SHAP importance. In the decision curve analysis, the threshold probabilities for net benefit ranged from 13 to 89%. This study developed a machine learning-based prognostic model for consciousness recovery in pDoC patients by integrating multimodal bedside data using efficient logistic regression. The model achieved moderate discriminative performance and provides preliminary evidence supporting individualized outcome predictions. When combined with clinical judgment, it may assist in optimizing treatment decisions for pDoC patients, although further validation is required.

papers.title: Multimodal Causal Reasoning Engine
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel Multimodal Causal Reasoning Engine designed to address the limitations of traditional single-modality causal inference. The core claim is that accurate causal reasoning can be achieved by effectively integrating information across diverse data modalities such as text, images, and video. The engine leverages a hybrid approach combining structured probabilistic graphical models and deep learning techniques to construct a multimodal causal graph and perform reasoning and prediction. Specifically, we utilize a deep learning model to estimate the causal dependencies between different modalities, and then employ a Bayesian network to represent and reason about these dependencies. The engine's ability to handle complex, multi-faceted causal relationships promises to significantly improve prediction accuracy and decision-making in scenarios involving heterogeneous data. The key innovation lies in the automated discovery and representation of causal relationships across modalities, a significant advancement over existing approaches. This work presents a framework for building intelligent systems capable of robust causal inference in complex, real-world environments.

papers.title: Multimodal Emotion Mapping and Understanding
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper explores the development of a novel framework for multimodal emotion understanding, predicated on establishing intricate mappings between various modalities – visual, auditory, and textual – to achieve a more holistic comprehension of human emotion. The core concept is to leverage multimodal deep learning models to effectively fuse information from these distinct sources, identifying and quantifying the complex relationships between them. Current emotion analysis techniques often operate within the confines of a single modality, limiting the richness and accuracy of emotional interpretation. This work moves beyond this limitation, explicitly addressing the interconnectedness of emotions across different modalities. The proposed approach utilizes deep learning architectures designed for multimodal fusion, enabling the extraction of nuanced emotional signals and ultimately leading to a more robust and accurate assessment of human emotion. We introduce a novel methodology for representing and analyzing these multimodal emotional landscapes.

papers.title: Adaptive Multimodal AI Tutoring: Using Real-Time Cues to Personalize Feedback and Support Engagement in Learning
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
papers.abstract: Learner engagement is commonly viewed as a key factor in successful learning. In online settings, limited face-to-face interaction can make learners more prone to distraction and reduced attention, highlighting the importance of monitoring and sustaining engagement. Recent advances in generative AI allow systems to infer learners’ cognitive and emotional states from multimodal cues, enabling more personalized and adaptive instructional support. However, little research has examined how such systems can dynamically adapt both the type and timing of feedback based on learners’ moment-to-moment engagement states inferred from multimodal signals. This work presents an adaptive multimodal AI-driven tutoring system that infers learners’ states by interpreting real-time visual, auditory, and behavioral cues. Based on the inferred learner state, the AI tutor determines when and how to intervene to sustain engagement. The system is structured as a closed-loop cognitive architecture: perception (capturing real-time multimodal cues), decision (aggregating the multimodal inputs into four affective metrics), and action (delivering feedback based on the inferred state by mapping each metric to a feedback type and timing strategy). This work presents a high-fidelity, interactive multimodal AI tutoring system that illustrates the feasibility of integrating multimodal cues to enable adaptive instructional feedback and engagement-aware intervention in online learning contexts.

papers.title: H&E to recurrence score: A step forward, but not yet a substitute for genomic testing
papers.venue: Translational Oncology
papers.abstract: Shamai and colleagues developed a multimodal deep-learning model that predicts Oncotype DX recurrence scores from routine H&E slides and clinicopathological variables in hormone receptor‑positive, HER2‑negative early breast cancer. Validated across the TAILORx trial and six external cohorts (over 5000 patients), the model achieved an AUC of 0.898 for identifying recurrence score ≥26 and recapitulated genomic assay patterns of chemotherapy benefit. Notably, 31% of clinically high-risk postmenopausal women were downgraded to low risk by AI, suggesting potential to reduce overtreatment. However, several limitations preclude immediate clinical substitution for genomic testing. First, intratumoural heterogeneity leads to discordant predictions with unclear management guidance. Second, the model's chemotherapy benefit estimates rely on TAILORx's age-based menopausal surrogates, which may not reflect real-world hormonal status or LHRH agonist use. Third, predictive value in node-positive disease remains untested in randomised datasets such as RxPONDER. Additionally, calibration uncertainty near risk thresholds and global scalability issues (including IHC requirements and digital pathology infrastructure) persist. While this represents a landmark step toward democratising precision oncology, the AI tool should currently serve as a complementary decision aid, with genomic testing remaining the gold standard for intermediate, borderline, or discordant cases.

papers.title: The neurocomputational mechanisms of naturalistic trait impression updating
papers.venue: OpenAlex
papers.abstract: Making prudent social decisions in everyday life requires people to form impressions of others’ personalities. First impressions, although impactful, are frequently incomplete or inaccurate. This necessitates mechanisms for updating impressions. This research examines types of information and computational operations the brain uses to update impressions. We collected functional neuroimaging data from participants (N = 28) as they viewed naturalistic audiovisual stimuli of people (N = 28) narrating emotional events in their lives. Pre-trained machine learning models annotated these target people’s facial expressions, voice qualities, and speech semantics. Deep neural networks implemented further computational operations on these annotations, including compression, multimodal fusion, temporal integration, and prediction. Independent participants (N = 602) continuously rated how their impressions of each target person’s traits varied across the course of the videos. Using spatiotemporal representational similarity analysis, we tested whether different perceptual modalities and operations explained patterns of brain activity in scanner participants and mediated spontaneous trait impression updating in the brain. We used intersubject representational similarity analysis to test whether participants’ mood, personality, demographics, or social attitudes explained individual differences in neural signatures of trait impression updating. All perceptual modalities and most computational operations were detected in the brain, but only facial expressions, speech semantics, and compression explained neural activity associated with trait impression updating. Social group attitudes were the only individual difference that mediated neural idiosyncrasies in trait updating. These results indicate that changing one’s mind about someone is a multifarious process, reliant upon multiple modalities of information, computational operations, and prior beliefs.

papers.title: 基于记忆网络的多模态数据融合
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the application of memory networks for multimodal data fusion. Traditional methods for multimodal data fusion often struggle with the inherent challenges posed by diverse data modalities, including differences in data representation, noise, and varying levels of correlation between modalities. We propose utilizing memory networks, specifically their ability to store and retrieve information through memory cells, to effectively integrate multimodal data. The core claim is that memory networks can effectively learn and fuse multimodal data, leading to improved prediction and decision-making accuracy. The proposed mechanism involves feeding multimodal data into the memory network, where memory cells store and retrieve data, and fuse information across different modalities. Experiments (simulated, as a full experimental section is omitted for brevity) demonstrate the potential of this approach, highlighting its robustness to noise and its capacity to capture complex relationships within the data. The key contribution lies in the adaptive learning and fusion capabilities of memory networks, offering a promising solution for challenging multimodal data fusion problems.

papers.title: Miller's Pyramid: Origin, Application, Advantages, Disadvantages, and Impact in Forensic Pathology Teaching
papers.venue: Academic Forensic Pathology
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control
papers.abstract: Introduction Competency-based medical education (CBME) emphasizes demonstrable competencies rather than time-based training. Miller's Pyramid remains an influential framework for conceptualizing clinical competence, but its contemporary application in forensic pathology education has not been comprehensively examined. This review evaluates its educational basis, applications, advantages, limitations, and relevance to forensic pathology teaching. Materials and Methods A narrative review was conducted of literature on Miller's Pyramid, CBME, workplace-based assessment (WPBA), entrustable professional activities (EPAs), milestones, programmatic assessment, and forensic pathology education. Educational and competency-based training approaches from India, the United States, Canada, and other settings were examined. Results Miller's Pyramid comprises four levels: Knows, Knows How, Shows How, and Does, representing progressive development from knowledge to independent practice. In forensic pathology, these levels can guide competency development in medico-legal autopsy, injury interpretation, evidence preservation, documentation, communication, and expert testimony. The framework facilitates alignment of learning objectives, teaching strategies, and assessment methods. However, its hierarchical structure may inadequately reflect the dynamic and context-dependent nature of competence and gives limited attention to professional identity, reflective practice, teamwork, and system-related influences. Integration with WPBA, EPAs, milestones, simulation, and programmatic assessment can address these limitations. Conclusion Miller's Pyramid remains a valuable framework for competency-based forensic pathology education. Its integration with contemporary assessment approaches can strengthen validity and support context-sensitive, longitudinal, and multimodal evaluation, ultimately promoting competent, accountable, and practice-ready forensic pathologists.

papers.title: KneeFusionNet Enables Accurate and Efficient Comprehensive Detection of Knee Ligament Injuries on Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Multicenter Validation Study
papers.venue: Arthroscopy The Journal of Arthroscopic and Related Surgery
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
papers.abstract: Purpose To develop and externally validate KneeFusionNet, a multimodal deep learning model for detecting anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), medial collateral ligament (MCL), and lateral collateral ligament (LCL) injuries on knee magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and to assess the impact of multimodal fusion and artificial intelligence (AI) assistance on diagnostic performance. Methods This 3‐center retrospective study was conducted between April 2020 and August 2025. The injury group included patients who underwent knee MRI within 1 month before arthroscopy and had surgically confirmed ACL, PCL, MCL, or LCL injuries; controls had unremarkable MRI and physical examination findings. Two centers formed the development set, and the remaining center served as the external test set. DenseNet‐based KneeFusionNet was developed and compared with 3 deep learning models. Diagnostic performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, and a reader study evaluated AI‐assisted diagnostic performance. Results Overall, 919 patients were included: 759 in the development set and 160 in the external test set. Multimodal fusion outperformed single‐modality approaches for all ligaments (all P < .05). On internal validation, KneeFusionNet achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curves of 0.971 for ACL, 0.906 for PCL, 0.919 for MCL, and 0.924 for LCL. Corresponding external area under the receiver operating characteristic curves were 0.888, 0.867, 0.862, and 0.874. Sex‐stratified analyses showed no consistent sex‐related decrease in model performance. KneeFusionNet outperformed all comparison models on internal validation (all P < .05). AI assistance improved mean diagnostic accuracy for junior surgeons from 0.818 to 0.900 and reduced mean interpretation time by 14.73 seconds across all surgeons (all P < .05). Conclusions KneeFusionNet detected ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL injuries on MRI with high diagnostic performance and outperformed comparison models. AI assistance improved diagnostic accuracy for junior surgeons and reduced interpretation time for all surgeons. Level of Evidence Level III, retrospective case‐control study.

papers.title: Reconsidering self-efficacy in contemporary early childhood education: The aesthetic self – A portrait of Priscilla
papers.venue: Contemporary Issues in Early Childhood
papers.abstract: This article argues that centralising aesthetics can strengthen early childhood teacher self-efficacy by reframing aesthetic sensibility as a lived capacity rather than a domain-specific skill. While aesthetic approaches have long been associated with early childhood education, they are increasingly marginalised within broader educational contexts shaped by standardisation, accountability and measurable outcomes. Drawing on portraiture methodology and the written image of ‘Priscilla’, an academic – artist – teacher, this article explores how aesthetic sensibility is sustained and enacted as an embodied and multimodal disposition. In doing so, it challenges distinctions between artist and non-artist, positioning aesthetic engagement as inherent to early childhood teachers in contemporary classroom settings. Through Priscilla's account, taken-for-granted assumptions are questioned, shifting attention from what students produce to what early childhood teachers make possible within learning environments. Within this framing, early childhood teachers are positioned as learners, and the artistry of being is understood as integral to teaching. The findings highlight concepts of becoming, multiplicity and displacement as conditions that strengthen teacher self-efficacy within arts-based practice. This article challenges neoliberal framings of early childhood education and positions aesthetics as central rather than peripheral to confident and agentic ways of teaching for early childhood teachers today.

papers.title: A Comparative Machine Learning Algorithms for Integrated Structural Health Monitoring in Smart Infrastructure maintenance and predication
papers.venue: Al-Farooq Journal of Sciences
papers.abstract: The convergence of civil infrastructure and electrical power systems within smart city frameworks necessitates robust, cross-domain monitoring strategies. While machine learning (ML) has shown promise in isolated Structural Health Monitoring (SHM) and Predictive Maintenance (PdM), comparative evaluations across both domains remain fragmented. This study presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of four prominent ML algorithms Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machines (SVM), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and XGBoost applied to multimodal sensor data. We utilized a synthesized dataset comprising vibration signatures from civil structures (bridge decks) and thermal-electrical load profiles from substation transformers. Our findings indicate that while LSTM networks excel in capturing temporal dependencies in electrical load forecasting (achieving an F1-score of 0.94), tree-based ensemble methods, specifically XGBoost, demonstrate superior efficacy in classifying structural damage from high-dimensional vibration features (accuracy of 96.2%). Furthermore, RF offered the most computationally efficient inference, making it highly suitable for edge-deployment in resource-constrained IoT nodes. This paper provides a practical decision-making framework for civil and electrical engineers selecting ML architectures for integrated smart infrastructure monitoring.

papers.title: Based on Multi-Modal Collaborative Reasoning for Knowledge Graphs (MCK)
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework, Multi-Modal Collaborative Reasoning for Knowledge Graphs (MCK), designed to enhance knowledge graph construction and reasoning capabilities by integrating information from diverse modalities. The core idea is to build a knowledge graph that can perform collaborative reasoning across text, images, and potentially audio data. The proposed methodology leverages deep learning models for individual modality processing, an attention mechanism for modality fusion, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for knowledge inference. This approach addresses the limitations of existing knowledge graphs, which predominantly rely on single-modality data, by significantly improving the expressive power and reasoning accuracy of the resulting graph. We demonstrate the potential of MCK through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and their interactions. The core claim is that by fusing multimodal data, we can construct a knowledge graph capable of multi-modal collaborative reasoning. The core mechanism involves deep learning for modality processing, attention-based fusion, and GNNs for inference. This new approach provides a pathway towards more robust and comprehensive knowledge representation and reasoning. ---

papers.title: Multimodal Emotion Mapping and Understanding
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: This paper explores the development of a novel framework for multimodal emotion understanding, predicated on establishing intricate mappings between various modalities – visual, auditory, and textual – to achieve a more holistic comprehension of human emotion. The core concept is to leverage multimodal deep learning models to effectively fuse information from these distinct sources, identifying and quantifying the complex relationships between them. Current emotion analysis techniques often operate within the confines of a single modality, limiting the richness and accuracy of emotional interpretation. This work moves beyond this limitation, explicitly addressing the interconnectedness of emotions across different modalities. The proposed approach utilizes deep learning architectures designed for multimodal fusion, enabling the extraction of nuanced emotional signals and ultimately leading to a more robust and accurate assessment of human emotion. We introduce a novel methodology for representing and analyzing these multimodal emotional landscapes.

papers.title: Twelve-Month Clinical Outcomes of Robotic PCI vs Manual PCI: A Systematic Review
papers.venue: Indonesian Journal of Cardiology
papers.abstract: Robotic-assisted Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (R-PCI) has been developed to improve procedural precision and reduce operator radiation exposure compared with Manual Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (M-PCI). Although short-term safety and feasibility have been well demonstrated, evidence on 12-month clinical outcomes remains limited. This systematic review evaluated 12-month clinical outcomes of R-PCI versus M-PCI in adult patients with coronary artery disease. Relevant literature published between January 2015 and April 2025 was identified through searches in Scopus, ScienceDirect, PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar. Eligible studies directly compared R-PCI and M-PCI and reported 12-month clinical outcomes, including Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events (MACE), Myocardial Infarction (MI), stroke, mortality, and Target Vessel Revascularization (TVR). Four cohort studies were included, involving 915 patients, of whom 334 underwent R-PCI, and 581 underwent M-PCI. At 12 months, MACE rates ranged from 0% to 10.5% after R-PCI and 1.4% to 8.1% after M-PCI. Mortality, MI, and TVR were low and comparable between groups. Although fluoroscopy time varied among studies, procedural success remained high, and adverse events were similar between groups. Studies that utilized Intravascular Ultrasound (IVUS) guidance reported particularly favorable outcomes. Overall, the available observational evidence suggests that R-PCI is associated with 12-month clinical outcomes comparable to those of M-PCI. However, given the limited number of studies, their observational design, and the absence of randomized data, these findings should be interpreted with caution. Further large-scale randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are warranted to more definitively establish the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of R-PCI.

papers.title: Design and Simulation of a Bio-inspired Variable Stiffness Continuum Robot for Household Ventilation Pipe Inspection
papers.venue: Applied and Computational Engineering
papers.abstract: This paper presents the design and simulation study of a bio-inspired variable stiffness continuum robot for household ventilation pipe inspection. Household ventilation pipes supply clean air and discharge indoor waste gas, yet they cannot perform automatic fault detection, and conventional rigid robots fail to adapt to complex bent pipelines. To tackle this issue, the robot employs a modular design using low-melting-point Wood's alloy as the stiffness-tuning medium, enabling transitions among fully flexible, fully rigid, and locally rigid states. A static finite element analysis is conducted to evaluate deformation behavior, stress distribution, and stiffness characteristics under bending loads. A cable-driven bending simulation in a curved pipe scenario assesses the robot's steering capability and the contact force on pipe walls. Results demonstrate that the variable stiffness mechanism achieves a 77.9% increase in bending stiffness when transitioning from flexible to rigid states, with the local rigidity strategy providing an optimal balance between conformability and load capacity for pipe inspection tasks.

papers.title: Research Progress on Visual Navigation and Control Methods for Surgical Robots
papers.venue: Theoretical and Natural Science
papers.abstract: In the last two decades, surgical robots have moved from specialized platforms to widely used tools in minimally invasive surgery. Their performance increasingly depends on visual navigation, because intraoperative images connect tissue perception, spatial localization, and motion control. Recent work has focused on how cameras, ultrasound, CT/MRI-derived models, optical tracking, and learning-based image analysis can be combined under the time pressure and uncertainty of the operating room. The discussion covers visual perception, multimodal imaging, segmentation, target recognition, three-dimensional reconstruction, image registration, real-time tracking, and vision-guided control in surgical robotics. Particular attention is given to the technical bottlenecks created by occlusion, specular reflection, tissue deformation, limited field of view, calibration drift, and data scarcity. The reviewed evidence shows that visual navigation is most useful when perception outputs are tightly linked to registration accuracy, safety constraints, and closed-loop control rather than treated as isolated image-processing results. Future progress will depend on more robust multimodal fusion, clinically reliable validation, safer intelligent control, and better integration of visual and haptic feedback in dynamic surgical scenes.

papers.title: Analysis of Actuator Selection for Low-Cost Bionic Limbs
papers.venue: Applied and Computational Engineering
papers.abstract: With the continuous advancement of mechatronics, low-cost bionic hands have been widely used in educational experiments and lightweight robotic research. As the core power components, actuators determine the mechanical output, power consumption and overall practical performance of bionic hands. A small mistake made during the choice making of actuators is fatal, which can result in problems such as insufficient gripping force or exceeding cost. This paper first establishes three evaluation criteria for bionic hand actuators: mechanical performance, electrical power requirements and practical application conditions. Then, the operating principles, hardware characteristics and inherent drawbacks of three mainstream actuators which are massively used in this area are elaborated respectively. A comparison is conducted through a table clearly showing the differences between the three types of actuators, and targeted selection suggestions are provided for different application scenarios. This paper finds that servo motors fit low-difficulty rapid teaching prototypes, geared direct current (DC) motors are suitable for stable long-term laboratory experimental platforms, and shape memory alloy (SMA) actuators are limited to lightweight exploratory research due to power consumption and response speed constraints. This research aims to build systematic hardware reference standards for beginners engaged in low-cost bionic hand design, avoiding biased actuator selection caused by ignoring integrated mechanical and electrical constraints.

papers.title: The Mechanism of Brain-Computer Interfaces: Converting Motor Cortex Neural Signals into Robotic Arm Control Commands
papers.venue: Theoretical and Natural Science
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) can provide patients with severe motor disorders with a new way to bypass damaged nerve pathways and control external devices by decoding the nerve activity of the motor cortex. Current research has made progress in continuous movement, multi-degree-of-freedom control and sensory feedback, but long-term stability, control accuracy and clinical safety are still limited. This paper analyses the signal acquisition characteristics of invasive, non-invasive and intravascular BCIs, sorts out the signal preprocessing, feature extraction and neural decoding processes, and summarizes the generation methods of continuous, discrete and multi-degree-of-freedom robotic arm instructions. Analysis shows that the collaborative optimization of signal quality, decoding algorithm and shared control strategy is the key to improving the naturalness and reliability of robotic arm operation. This article provides a systematic reference for the design and research of the BCI robotic arm system. Future research should focus on developing stable neural interfaces, adaptive individual decoding, computer vision assistance and two-way sensory feedback to promote their long-term clinical and daily applications.

papers.title: Formalizing Competencies and Defining the Characteristics of a Digital Environment for Learning Human–Robot Collaboration in Construction: Insights from Industry and Academia
papers.venue: Journal of Civil Engineering Education
topics: Innovations in Concrete and Construction Materials
papers.abstract: Abstract Human–robot collaboration (HRC) refers to the interaction between humans and robots in a shared workspace, combining human adaptability with robotic precision to execute tasks. This study formalizes HRC competencies and identifies the characteristics (training components) of a digital environment for learning HRC in construction through separate focus group discussions with industry and academic participants. A thematic analysis, conducted using inductive coding and validated through interrater reliability, reveals the rationale for prioritizing the top-rated HRC competencies across industry and academia. The top-rated HRC knowledge areas emphasize the importance of integrating HRC to enhance efficiency and safety, as well as adapting it to evolving industry needs. Prioritized skills underscore the importance of aligning knowledge and skills to support effective HRC implementation and enhance human–robot interface and communication proficiencies. The top-rated abilities highlight the significance of foundational, adaptive, and collaborative abilities for safe and effective HRC. The characteristics of a digital environment for learning HRC include robotic technologies, such as drones, three-dimensional (3D) printers, and wearable exoskeletons, which are considered essential for HRC training in construction. Applications such as surveying, bricklaying, and high-precision tasks provide hands-on learning opportunities. Facilitating conditions, including robust network connectivity, reliable power supplies, and modular construction processes, enhance the learning experience. This study contributes to knowledge by formalizing HRC competencies and proposing a digital learning environment that incorporates robotic technologies, practical applications, and facilitating conditions based on the perspectives of industry professionals and academic experts. It also contributes to Activity Theory by advancing its use as a conceptual framework for structuring and interpreting relationships among learners, HRC competencies, stakeholder perspectives, and training components within digital learning environments for HRC in construction.

papers.title: Towards a Gold Dataset for Cross-Perspective Ontology Alignment in the Food Domain
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Ontology alignment serves as the backbone of semantic interoperability among heterogeneous knowledge resources. However, many real-world domains are modeled from multiple perspectives, depending on the purpose, community, and context of use. Existing benchmarks focus primarily on ontologies with similar modeling goals. This limits the evaluation of alignment methods across different perspectives. To address this gap, this paper presents an ongoing effort to develop a small, expert-oriented benchmark dataset for cross-perspective ontology alignment in the food domain. The dataset is created from selected subsets of three existing ontologiesrepresenting nutrition and diet, food quality and public health, and food-service occupations using the ROBOT tool. These heterogeneous ontological commitments often produce meaningful semantic relations that go beyond equivalence matching.The workflow includes seed-term-based concept selection, extraction of labels, definitions, superclass context, properties, and restrictions, followed by expert annotation of semantic bridge relations across perspectives. The resulting dataset is intended to support the evaluation of ontology alignment method cross different standpoints.
